SCOPE_NOTE: Sites, buildings, structures, features and areas of land associated with cultivation, the rearing of livestock, gathering, hunting & fishing. Includes farm based processing of foodstuffs & storage of agricultural produce.
A building used for an agricultural and/or subsistence purpose. Use more specific type where known.
A building where animals are slaughtered.
A small outlying farm building, especially common in southern England, used to store ash (which was used as a fertilizer).
A building for the storage and processing of grain crops and for housing straw, farm equipment and occasionally livestock and their fodder. Use more specific type where known.
A levelled area of ground on which a barn is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a barn.
A large barn used to store the tithe (a tenth part of the annual produce of agriculture etc.) which was paid by the tenants of ecclesiastical lands.
A building, or part of a building, for the milling and pressing of cider apples to produce cider (or pears for perry) and for storing the drink in barrels.
A HORSE GIN used for domestic cider manufacture, especially on farms.
A mill for grinding corn. Use with power type where known.
A place where meat and fruit, etc, is preserved by salting and/or drying.
A building or group of buildings used for the making, processing, storing and selling of milk and other dairy products.
A building, or part of a building, used to house doves and pigeons, usually placed at a height above the ground, with openings and provision inside for roosting and breeding.
A building used to accommodate ducks.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A building, or first-floor room in a building, for the dry and secure storage of grain after it has been threshed and winnowed.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A building with malt kilns for the malting of grains and with other similar equipment for brewing work.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
An enclosure for pigs that includes a covered pen and yard.
A structure providing accommodation for poultry.
A building providing shelter for sheep and storage for fodder and shepherding equipment.
Pasture to which animals were driven for grazing, with associated temporary huts for domestic or agricultural use.
A mill which contains machinery for separating grain from the chaff.
A place where beehives are kept.

A recess in a stone or brick wall, usually bounding a garden or orchard, set two to three feet from the ground and facing south to south-east to catch the morning sun, in which a bee skep/beehive is placed. Often found in groupings of three to six.
A garden in which bees are kept.
A receptacle used as a home for bees, traditionally made of thick straw-work in the shape of a dome, but sometimes made of wood.
A wall built to give shelter to sheep.
A press used to extract the juice from apples, which was then used to make cider.
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.
A heated stone, brick or iron chamber used for drying corn.
A shallow pond, often artificial, fed by the condensation of water from the air, occuring on high land which has no other adequate water supply.
A yard or enclosure attached to a farmhouse, usually surrounded by other farm buildings.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.
Underground passage with storage chambers found in South West England.
A building, site or structure associated with the hunting of animals.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A building for housing deer overnight.
Bank to let deer cross ditches, fences or roads, into, but not out of, a deer park.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A building used to shelter deer hunters.
An establishment or building where the breeding and training of birds of prey takes place.
An area where fish are naturally present, eg. part of a river.
A holding tank/pen on a river or seashore for raising and preserving fish and/or for catching them easily.
A device for catching fish, may be a portable or permanent structure, often a fence or row stakes made in a river, harbour, etc
A fence or row of stakes, often with nets attached forming an enclosure within a river or harbour and used for catching, or holding, fish.

A structure comprising of two walls of stone or wood with nets or fish traps attached. Located in coastal waters, on shelving coastlines or in river estuaries they form large enclosures with a V or L shaped plan. The narrow point on the seaward side.
A mound used to elevate buildings associated with a fishery e.g. smoke houses, above the level of a flood plain.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic temporary site where there is evidence to suggest animal butchery. Evidence may include animal remains and a specialized tool assemblage.
A free-standing building with enough space to hang and dry nets.
A component of another building, often a house, used for storing nets.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
Position often screened by earth, stone or wood from which game is shot.
A stone-lined pit in which seaweed was burnt. The calcined ashes were used in the manufacture of soap and glass, amongst other things.
A share or portion of land, allotted to a person, often used for growing, vegetables, fruit, etc.
A monument featuring a bank or mound constructed primarily of stone. Use specific type where known.
An irregularly constructed, generally unstructured, mound of stones. Often, but not necessarily, circular. Normally a by product of field clearance for agricultural purposes.
A group of cairns occurring within close proximity to each other. Use for instances where the majority are clearance cairns. Also index specific types where known.
Unenclosed wasteland, forest and pasture used in common by the community.
An enclosed piece of land adjoining a house.
Manmade marks or earthworks which provide evidence for agricultural cultivation.
The subsoil traces of cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of a plough to till the soil.
An area of land, usually on a slope, which has been built up to provide a flat surface for the cultivation of crops.
A tract of land, often including a farmhouse and ancillary buildings, used for the purpose of cultivation and the rearing of livestock, etc. Use more specific type where known.
The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
An area of land, often enclosed, used for cultivation or the grazing of livestock.
Narrow ridges representing the surviving surface traces of later prehistoric cultivation.
The limit line of a field.
A bank formed at the end of a field by soil which, loosened by the plough, gradually moves down slope through a combination of gravity and erosion.
A narrow strip of land where a plough and team could turn. This usually remains higher than the ploughed land.
A series of long, raised ridges separated by ditches used to prepare the ground for arable cultivation. This was a technique, characteristic of the medieval period.
Long parallel soil ridges in excess of 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
Long parallel soil ridges less than 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
A ridge and furrow produced by a plough drawn between two steam engined vehicles, or a steam engined vehicle and a moveable windlass, standing on opposite headlands.
A terraced field usually found on hillsides. Comprising a flat strip of land, called the tread, and a steep, scarped lynchet or edge, called the riser.
A group or complex of fields which appear to form a coherent whole. Use more specific type where known.
A field system which appears to have developed in an organic, or piecemeal, fashion over time.

A fairly regular system of small rectangular fields. Examples may date from the middle Bronze Age to the Roman period. The word 'Celtic' carries no chronological or cultural connotations in this context.
An area of land which retains distinctive large-scale rectilinear land divisions characteristic of Roman agriculture. Generally aligned with the course of a Roman road.
A field system with one prevailing axis of orientation, in which most field boundaries are either aligned with this axis or run at right angles to it.
A system of individually enclosed fields.
An area of arable land with common rights after harvest or while fallow. Usually without internal divisions (hedges, walls or fences).
Grassland fertilized by allowing floodwater to cover it in winter.
An enclosed piece of ground devoted to the cultivation of flowers, fruit or vegetables and/or recreational purposes. Use more specific type where known.
A piece of land used for the cultivation of hops.
A private garden established primarily for growing vegetables and herbs for domestic consumption.
A piece of land used to grow vegetables to be sold at markets.
A horticultural site where trees, shrubs and plants are grown for sale and transplanting elsewhere.

An outlying farm or estate, usually belonging to a religious order or feudal lord. Specifically related to core buildings and structures associated with monastic land holding. Use specific term where known.
Areas used for potato-growing.
An area of land consisting of the lord's demesne and of lands from whose holders he may exact certain fees, etc.
An enclosure used for the cultivation of fruit trees.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a plantation.
A system of long, continuous banks and/or ditches dividing land into well defined areas. Possibly used for controlling livestock

A stone wall, often of considerable length, built to divide an area of land. Most occur as part of extensive walled field systems. This is a regional term specific to Dartmoor and should not be used in other parts of the country.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
An area of land and associated buildings where vines are cultivated. The grapes produced are then used to make wine.
A cultivated plantation of watercress, usually situated near springs or small running streams.
A tract of land with trees, sometimes acting as a boundary or barrier, usually smaller and less wild than a forest.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a wood or coppice
A place where oysters are bred for consumption.
A pillow-shaped, flat topped rectangular mound often surrounded by a shallow ditch used to farm rabbits.
A pen, often circular and stone-walled, for rounding up livestock.
An area used for the breeding and rearing of rabbits.
A place where sheep are washed in a chemical bath to control  the parasites of sheep. To conserve the poisonous chemicals the bath is usually small and are not allowed to enter any watercourse.
A pen or enclosure used for containing sheep.
A refuse heap of discarded shells.
A platform for storing winter fodder.
Mushroom-shaped stones used to raise the floor of barns, granaries etc. above ground level, to prevent vermin gaining access to stored grain and fodder.
A pound for the accommodation of livestock.
A pit dug in the ground used to store meat, grain and other foodstuffs. A common feature of Iron Age farms.
A pit where grain is stored.
A place where swans are bred and reared.
An area of a barn, paved or boarded, on which corn was threshed by hand flailing. Use broader site type where known.
A structure used to dry turf on. Turves were used as a fuel and as a roofing material.
A device used to trap or kill animals considered to be pests, eg. rats.
A pen for holding sheep waiting to be washed.

Sites, buildings, structures etc associated with the civil administration of settlements & enforcement of the laws of the land. Includes local & central government, settlements granted by the crown or ruling administration does not manorial settlements.
A hall in which public assemblies and meetings can be held.
An aisled timber or masonry hall, serving as the chief administrative public meeting centre and law courts for a Roman town. Usually located alongside the forum.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A hall associated with a church, used for holding functions, meetings and for conducting parish business.
House owned by the church, often used for meetings.
Civil building in Cornwall and Devon for assay and sale of tin ingots.
A box in which letters are posted or deposited for dispatch.
A building, department or shop where postal business is carried on.
A signal station incorporating equipment for visually conveying coded communications.

A building or tower used to communicate information to shipping or other stations using signals such as flags, fires or lights. Roman signal stations took the form of a stone tower surrounded by a ditched enclosure and were used to warn of Saxon raids.
A place where letters and parcels are sorted before being distributed. Usually found at a large general post office.

One in a chain of stations with semaphore shutters and telescopes which could relay messages according to a planned code. Used from the 1790s by the British Admiralty to speed up communications from London to the ports of Deal, Portsmouth and Plymouth.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
An office or central station of a local telephone system where the various lines are brought to a central switchboard and communication between subscribers is achieved.
A building from which the administration of a county is carried out by the County Council. It is also, historically, the site where the county quarter sessions and assizes were held.
Sites, buildings, structures & features relating to the provision of knowledge and skills.
A building in which works of art are displayed, permanently or temporarily.
An establishment, often forming part of a university, for higher or tertiary education.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A building, room or suite of rooms where books, or other materials, are classified by subject and stored for use by the library's members.
A building, group of buildings or space within a building, where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artefacts are housed and displayed.
A building containing celestial telescopes in which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
An establishment in which people, usually children, are taught.
A school founded in or before the 16th century, for teaching Latin, later becoming a secondary school teaching languages, history, science, etc.
A school for instruction in the art of horsemanship.
A group of colleges and associated buildings belonging to a university.
A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which wild animals are kept and reared for public exhibition.
A large, rectangular open space at the centre of a Roman town, incorporating public spaces and a market area.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with health (for example, treatment of the sick) &/or social welfare (for example, alleviation of poverty), including all charitable foundations & all forms of state defined social welfare.
A building adjacent to a monastery where alms were distributed to the poor.
A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
A building where ambulances are housed awaiting emergency calls.
A building, usually open to the public, containing a number of areas for bathing. In the case of such a complex containing baths for swimming, also index with INDOOR or OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL.
An institution, sometimes attached to a hospital, where patients may receive treatment or health checks.
A building or group of buildings situated close to the sea used by coastguards to enable them to monitor the coastline.
A civic building housing fire engines and a permanent fire-fighting force.
An establishment providing medical or surgical treatment for the ill or wounded. Use narrower term where possible.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.
A stone on which plague victims placed vinegar-disinfected money to pay for food left for them by the townspeople.
A hospital for convalescents or consumptives.
A medicinal or mineral spring often with an associated building.

A 19th century establishment for the provision of work for the unemployed poor of a parish; later an institution administered by Guardians of the Poor, in which paupers are lodged and the able-bodied set to work.
A building in which a judicial court is held.
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
A chair fixed to the end of a plank, in which scolds or dishonest people were tied and ducked in water as a punishment.
A place where people were put to death. Use narrower monument type where known.
A structure used for execution by hanging. Usually two uprights and a cross-piece, from which the offender is suspended by the neck.
A natural or man-made earth mound on which a gallows was erected.
An upright post with projecting arm from which the body of a criminal would be hung in chains after execution.
A place where a yearly or half-yearly court of record is held by lords of certain manors.
A wooden frame with holes, through which the head and hands of an offender were thrust, in which state they would be exposed to public ridicule and assault.
The office or headquarters of a local police force, or of a police district.
An establishment where offenders are confined. Use more specific type where known.
An elevated platform on which a criminal is executed.
An instrument of punishment, in which the offender was placed in a sitting position in a timber frame, with holes to confine the ankles and wrists between two planks.
A post set up, to which offenders were tied to be whipped.
A type of guildhall belonging primarily to the London livery companies, but also found elsewhere in the country, so called because of the livery worn by members of the guild.
A type of Roman lodging house, frequently sited near the town gate.
A place where money is coined under public authority.
An outdoor meeting place.
A meeting hall, sometimes equivalent to a GUILDHALL, but also associated with some early mining industries.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
The limit line of a parish.
A hall built for the use of people living within a parish boundary.
A building or group of buildings owned and operated by a governing body and often occupied by a government agency. Use specific type of building where known.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
A planned administrative capital for local government which provided amenities for the Roman and peregrine (non-Roman) inhabitants of the town.
A town founded as an act of government by charter to house Roman or Latin citizens, usually retired legionaires who had been granted land within a territorium.
A town for citizens of Roman or Latin status with a constitution governed by charter, which if possessing only Latin rights could be promoted to the status of a colonia.
A large building used for the transaction of the public business of a town, the holding of courts of justice, entertainments and other activities.
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
A hall in a village used for meetings and other functions.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land commemorating an historical event, person or animal.
The field or area of ground on which a battle or skirmish was fought.
A sepulchral monument erected to commemorate a person or persons buried elsewhere.
An inscribed marker stone found on Hadrian's Wall.
Use both terms.
Includes crests, hatchments and supporters.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
A building, structure or landscape created to commemorate a person or event.
A stone commemorating the date of a specific event.
A commemorative stone inscribed with a dedicatory inscription to a person or event.
A giant figure of a man, animal or symbol carved on chalk hillsides mainly in southern England.
Site with important historical association.
A structure, building or site commemorating soldiers and civilians killed in war.
Use both terms.
A tree named after a person or event associated with it, e.g. Byron's Oak at Newstead.
A tall, tapering pillar with a pyramidal top, generally square on plan. Used in England from the late 16th century as a public, funerary or garden monument.
A representation in the round of a living being, allegorical personage, eminent person or animal, etc, sculptured, moulded or cast in marble, metal, plaster, etc.
A large free-standing arch erected to commemorate a triumph or victory.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the sale, exchange &/or storage of goods or services. Includes commercially operated catering establishments & lodging premises.
A building for the weighing or testing of metals, eg. at a mine site.
A commercial bakery or bread factory. If domestic use BAKEHOUSE.
A cheap eating and drinking establishment usually serving snacks and non-alcoholic drinks.
Traditionally the premises of a chandler, a maker and seller of candles. Now, a shop for the retail of groceries and other provisions.
A market hall where cloth merchants can show their wares and conduct business.
An establishment serving coffee and other refreshments and inexpensive foods. Between the 17th and 18th centuries they were also meeting places for political discussions.
An accounts office, especially within an industrial or commercial complex.
A multi-purpose commercial building, used primarily as a trading place for merchants, but also incorporating shops, public offices, guildhalls, etc.
A building where samples of corn were sold or auctioned during the early to mid 19th century. When not in use, between market days, the buildings were used as public halls.
A building which provides the centralized market for trading in stocks and shares and for raising capital for industry.
A site where a periodical gathering of buyers, sellers and entertainers, meet at a time ordained by charter or statute or by ancient custom.
A stone slab, raised on stone or wooden piers, used for the display of fresh fish. Usually found in market places.
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
A large building used for the accommodation of paying travellers and guests.
A public house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers, etc.
A public house offering lodgings to the passengers, and stabling for the horses of stage coaches.
A room or building where clothing and other fabrics are washed, mangled, steamed and ironed.
An open space or covered building in which cattle, goods, etc, are displayed for sale.
A market where cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry are bought and sold.
A purpose built covered market hall, usually 19th century, although earlier examples do exist, eg. that at Abingdon, Oxfordshire c.1680.
An area, often consisting of widened streets or a town square, where booths and stalls may be erected for public sales.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
A place where refreshments or meals may be obtained.
Traditionally a place where meat and fish were sold.
A house or building where goods are made or prepared and displayed for sale and sold. Use more specific type where known.
A covered shopping street, sometimes with galleries, dating from the late 18th/early 19th century.
A hiding place for stores, often underground, used by smugglers.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of goods or merchandise. Use more specific type where known.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of wine.

Sites, buildings, structures & features used in the defence of the civilian population. Includes civil defence sites, weapons stores, training sites, military signals & active defence structures such as anti-aircraft sites.
A fortified structure used to protect civilians and military personnel from enemy bombing.
An oval or circular structure with seats rising in tiers around a central open space. Used for religious ceremonies, entertainment, training and armed combat contests.
A fortified tower found at the angle of a castle wall.
A building used to store military equipment and ammunition.
A place where weapons are kept.
A building or large scale site for the manufacture and/or storage of weapons, ammunition and equipment.
A place in which the artillery is encamped or collected together.
A fortified tower designed to house a number of artillery pieces and a small garrison. Artillery towers first appear in England in the 16th century.
Any earthworks, walling, bastion or fortified outwork, or combination of these, generally with ditch or moat.
A defensive cattle enclosure added to fortified towers.
A building used to house members of the armed forces.
A flanking tower, or projection from the main walls of a defensive work from which a garrison can defend the ground in front or on the flank.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.
A site where guns, mortars or searchlights are mounted. Use specific type where known.
A site containing one or more artillery pieces and/or rocket launchers for firing at enemy aircraft.
A site in which one or more searchlights were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
A site or structure on which a signal, especially a fire, could be placed as a warning or means of communication. Use for beacon sites or surviving beacon structures.
A detached fort covering a strategic point.
A temporary fieldwork, usually a few feet in height, constructed for defence against enemy forces.
A mound or structure on which an archery, musketry or artillery target is erected. Use specific type where known.
A mound or structure on which targets are placed for archery practice or competition.
A target range used for rifle and small arms practice and recreational purposes.
A fortress and dwelling, usually medieval in origin, and often consisting of a keep, curtain wall and towers etc.
A castle erected without permission, ie. without a royal licence to crenellate.
Castles constructed between 1481 and 1561 for defence using heavy guns.
The courtyard of a castle, ie. the area enclosed by the rampart or curtain. Use with wider site type where known.
A castle surrounded by two or more lines of walled fortifications.
The major tower of a fortification, often acting as its last defence.
A Norman keep, in the form of a circular or polygonal enclosure surrounded by a wall.
A fortified keep in the form of a tower, used as a last refuge or defence. If a component of a larger site, use KEEP.
An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.
An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.
A castle built on a simple, rectangular plan, usually with a tower at each corner. This design became common in England after 1300.
A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.
An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
A temporary castle built to house and protect troops beseiging another castle or town.
A system of stones or wooden obstacles placed close together to impede the advance of enemy forces. Do not use for HILLFORT sites.
A dome shaped building, housing training apparatus, including a projector, for training ground gunners in the art of airfield defence.  (WWII).
A building or site used for the exercise and training of military personnel.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A multiple, parallel arrangement of linear earthwork ditches, usually accompanied by banks, and often of considerable territorial extent. Usually of later prehistoric or Roman date.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.
An enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a promontory which projects into the sea.
A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.
A usually temporary earthwork or fortification, the latter constructed by military forces operating in the field. Use more specific type where known.
A piece of ground over which small arms or large artillery may be fired at targets. For rocket and missile firing use ROCKET TEST FACILITY.
A permanently occupied position or building designed primarily for defence.
A fortified building or site with purpose built emplacements for artillery pieces.
A permanent Roman fort enclosed by a number of ditches and ramparts, used to house a garrison of auxiliaries.
A small enclosure built onto the perimeter of a Roman fortress or fort.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.
A military base normally between 20 and 30 acres in size, containing legionary and auxiliary battle units, which served as stores depots and winter quarters during campaigns.
A usually permanent defensive work. Use specific type where known.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
A fortified Roman site, usually under 1 hectare in area, strategically situated, housing small military patrols, often defended by a rampart, one or two ditches and a gate.
A small, walled fortlet, situated every Roman mile along the length of Hadrian's Wall to defend a gateway allowing the passage of people and as a garrison to accommodate patrol troops.
A free standing small turf and timber fortlet, situated every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A major fortified place, often a town, capable of containing a large force. If Roman use LEGIONARY FORTRESS.
A large, fortified permanent Roman military base, made of timber and stone, surrounded by a rampart and ditches.

A system of fortifications constructed along a national frontier to contain the local population, as well as keep out undesirable raiders eg. Offa's Dyke. Use with more specific monument type where known.

A small tower or bartizan, which was often placed at the angles of a castle, to increase the flanking ability, some only serving as corner buttresses. Also used to describe the small rectangular towers situated between the milecastles along Hadrians Wall.
A flat bottomed ditch flanked by mounds running to the south of Hadrian's Wall for much of its length, marking the boundary of the military zone.
A building used for the accommodation of a military guard and/or the detainment of prisoners.
A fortified site in which a gun, mortar or cannon is positioned.
A sunken arena used by the Romans for training cavalry horses and recruits.

A tower situated above the rampart walkway and in between the angle towers along a defensive structure, such as a castle wall. They were used as lookout towers, roofed strongpoints or platforms from which missiles could be discharged or artillery fired.
A site equipped with instruments or structures, such as sound mirrors, to listen for the approach of enemy aircraft
A substantial bank and ditch forming a major boundary between two adjacent landholdings. Most date from the late Bronze Age and Iron Age.
A building in which a supply of arms, ammunition and provisions for an army is stored.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A coastal gun/watch tower built as part of the anti-invasion defences during the Napoleonic Wars.
A building or group of buildings, often surrounded by a system of fortifications, used as a residential and training site by members of an armed force.
A site where a body of troops is temporarily or permanently lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
An enclosure of stakes driven into the ground, sometimes for defensive purposes.
A place where military personnel parade, practice marching, assemble or muster for a march or any other special purpose.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.

An often squat building with thick, loopholed walls and a flat roof, designed to accommodate a variety of weapons, usually strategically positioned to cover a vulnerable point in a defensive system. Many were built to standardized designs.
A small gateway cut through the curtain wall or its flanking towers. Used primarily as an outlet for counter-attacking forces.
A prison site for the containment of servicemen captured in war.
A building or site incorporating equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy aircraft or ships. Radar Stations can also be used to aid aircraft navigation in dark or poor conditions.
A protective earthen mound, often the main defence of a fortification.
A small protective fortification, such as an earthwork.
A temporary earthwork or fortification constructed by forces laying siege to a castle or town, etc.
A covered trench, often in a zig zag form, made for the purpose of approaching a beseiged place under fire of the garrison.
Reinforced concrete blocks, walls or ditches designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A temporary overnight camp enclosed by a shallow ditch and palisade, constructed by Roman troops on campaigns or manoeuvres.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
Defensive fortifications such as ramparts, ditches and stone walls, built to defend a town or city.
A highly defensible gateway, usually of stone with two or more storeys, built into the defensive walls of a town or city.
An excavation used as a means of concealment, protection or both.
A short trench used to protect troops or to provide defensive fire from, often dug for practice purposes.
A building or structure from which observation is kept of the approach of danger.
A gate leading to water, either a river or the sea. Used as a means of supplying castles, for example, with goods brought by water transport.

Sites, buildings, structures and features used for permanent, seasonal or temporary accommodation/habitation & related ancillary buildings. Includes commercial, military and religious sites used for residential purposes as well as industrial workplaces.
A pit containing burnt ashes.
A service building to a country house, farm, etc, used for baking. If commercial premises use BAKERY.
Small building in which labourers, such as miners and tin workers. They are also associated with gardens where they provide on-site accommodation for gardeners and estate workers.

A mound of fire-cracked stones, normally accompanied by a trough or pit which may have been lined with wood, stone or clay. Assumed to be locations where heated stones were used to boil water primarily for cooking purposes.
A small building in which game is hung up and kept cool.

A timber building based around a sunken hollow, the floor of which may have been suspended above the hollow to counteract dampness. Grubenhauser are believed to date from the 5th to 8th centuries AD but may be earlier. Use Grubenhauser as plural.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.
Residences of religious people and members of the clergy.
The official residence of a bishop.
A residence for all clergy having the sole or subordinate charge of a living.
The official residence of a dean.
A non-conformist minister's house.
The residence of a priest.
The residence of a vicar, parson or rector.

A building or buildings ranged around a courtyard on at least three sides. They occur in the Iron Age, as well as being an influential plan type of house from the 15th century onwards. Index with appropriate period.
An island, partly or wholly artificial, built up by dumping timber, earth and stones onto a lake or river bed. Often revetted with timber piles or palisade.
A large house dating from the 16th century onwards, built as a symbol of the wealth and status of the owner but not intended to be defensible unlike the castles and manor houses it replaced.
The rural residence of a country gentleman.
The principal house of a manor or village.
A substantial house in a town or the country (particularly associated with medieval London). Use more specific monument types where known.
A large, luxuriously appointed building used as an official residence by a member of royalty.
An area of ground on which a house is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a house.

A tower or structure, with a powerful light or lights at the top, usually erected at an important or dangerous point on or near the sea-coast for the warning and guidance of mariners, but can also be erected inland for the guidance of travellers.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
A dwelling built on marshy, boggy or waterlogged land using timber piles driven vertically into the ground to raise the floor above the ground to prevent flooding.
A dwelling cut into the rockface of a cliff or hillside, often with a built frontage. Many date from the Medieval period and are still in use in some areas of the country.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
A gentry house in a town or city, either detached or in a terrace.

A building of basic construction, usually smaller in size than a house and constructed from a variety of materials such as mud, turf, branches, wood, brick, concrete or metal. Use more specific type where known.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A crude shelter for persons engaged in the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.

A round house indicated by the presence of a low, roughly circular bank of turf, earth or stone, which formed the base of the walls. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Where several occur together use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT.
Levelled or terraced area of ground presumed to have been the site of a house or hut.
A hut used by a person who makes items from wood. Often found in a woodland setting.

A Roman under-floor heating system in which hot air heated by a stoked furnace, flowed through channels, created by either raising the floor on pillars of brick and tile or cutting channels into the concrete floor and tiling over them.
A building or room where food is prepared and cooked.
A small building, often inhabited by a gatekeeper, gamekeeper or similar. Use specific type where known.
A dwelling, located at the entrance, or gates, to an estate or park, etc.
A refuse heap.
A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.
The area beneath a natural overhang at the base of a cliff or crag. This may have been used for occupation, burial, etc. Index with site type where known.
A pit where domestic waste material is deposited.
A house for storing or drying saddles.
A small concentration of dwellings.
Temporary settlement relating to the construction of railways, viaducts, dams, etc.

A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.

A small rectangular or sub circular area or areas bounded by an earthwork, ditch or similar boundary, where one side is formed by an existing linear boundary, forming a pattern reminiscent of clothes hanging from a washing line.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
Use both terms.
A small, defensive settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling and ancillary buildings, surrounded by a palisade.
A settlement site enclosed within a timber palisade.
Small settlement with no ecclesiastical or lay administrative function.

A settlement consisting of several hut circles, either grouped together or dispersed. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Use specific forms where supported by the available evidence. For isolated hut circles use HUT CIRCLE.

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
A group of related buildings, primarily with a domestic function, which is arranged along a principle axis such as a main road or routeway.
A community of Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines, first founded by Moravian emigrants in Saxony, Germany.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic occupation site, excluding occupations of caves and rock shelters. Evidence for occupation may include traces of hearths and other structures.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
A settlement, usually enclosed, on a sloping hillside containing a number of oval or circular scopped house floors separated by walls or unexcavated ridges.
An underground chamber, store room or passage.
Underground chambers and stone passages of Iron Age date found in South West England.
A parcel of land.
A settlement without any obvious evidence for a boundary. Use specific type where known.
A settlement located on or near to the shores of a lake. Buildings associated with lake villages are usually raised on piles to prevent them from being flooded.
Small discreet rural settlements which do not provide the commercial, legal or ecclesiastical services typically found within medieval urban areas.
A collection of dwelling-houses and other buildings, usually larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town with a simpler organisation and administration than the latter.
A settlement whose plan suggests the aggregation of several formerly distinct settlement nuclei into a single settlement.

The site of a deserted settlement in cases where there is evidence that it has deliberately been relocated in a single planned action, eg. to remove a settlement from an enclosed park, or to create a model community, as opposed to gradual abandonment.
An extant settlement which shows evidence of a shift in focus, eg. towards a new road, generally in the form of abandoned buildings or earthworks on the margin furthest from the new focus.
A settlement where previous house sites are now unoccupied, but often visible as earthworks, crop or soil marks.
A house, enclosure or large cage for the keeping and breeding of birds.
A platform or other structure for the use of a band of musicians.
A turret, tower or look out occupying a prominent position to provide a view, either a separate building, or part of a villa.
An artificial fall of water often taking the form of a water staircase.
A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.

A structure, often found in 18th century landscape gardens, that demonstrates eccentricity or excess rather than practical purpose. They can take many forms - ruins, sham castles, towers, hermits' cells or grottoes.

An artificial aperture from which water springs. The water supply usually came from a lake or reservoir higher up in order to ensure the necessary flow and pressure. More recently fountains have been powered by pumps.
A fountain erected specifically to supply drinking water.
An often highly elaborate water fountain, usually found in parks, gardens or urban spaces.
A garden of regular, linear or geometrical design, often associated with the traditional Italian, French and Dutch styles.
A small ornamental building in a garden, usually one-storeyed and consisting of one room. Use a more specific term where known.
A garden building, usually in the Gothic or classical style. The term can be applied to many types of garden building with an interior space in which to stand or sit. Use specific type where known.
A stone or brick wall either in, or enclosing, a garden.
A garden house situated to provide a commanding view.
A shady cavern built as a garden feature. In the 18th century it usually took the form of an artificial rocky cave or apartment decorated with stalactites and shells in a wild part of the grounds.
A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.

A confusing and baffling network of winding and intercommunicating paths, often bordered by high hedges or walls. Some early examples are believed to have had ritual uses. Use more specific type where known.
A complex maze incorporating tall hedges. A popular feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.
An artificial stretch of water, usually rectangular in shape, used decoratively, particularly in formal gardens, eg. Long Water, Hampton Court. Occasionally used to supply water to cascades.
An artificial lake, often made by damming a stream. A common feature of landscape parks.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A tall, polygonal structure with ornamental roofs at each storey which is associated with Buddhist temples; the style was adapted for secular eyecatchers and pavilions in the 18th century in England.
An enclosed piece of land, generally large in area, used for hunting, the cultivation of trees, for grazing sheep and cattle or visual enjoyment. Use more specific type where known.
Grounds, usually associated with a country house, laid out so as to produce the effect of natural scenery.
A park for the use of the public for entertainment and relaxation.
A stone or brick wall enclosing a park.
A light, sometimes ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation, used for entertainment or shelter. Use specific type where known.
Timber or metal structure consisting of upright and cross members designed to support climbing plants.
An area attached to a house, or part of an estate used for pleasure and recreation.
An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
A tower built on a prominent part of an estate to provide panoramic views of the surrounding countryside.
An isolated building, circular in plan, generally consisting of one apartment with a domed roof, eg. Mausoleum at Castle Howard, Yorkshire.
A straight road lined with trees along either side, also straight lines of trees found in parkland usually leading to a landscape feature.

A circular bank in which trees have been planted for ornamental purposes or to create an enclosure. May exist purely as a bank which has been formed over the stumps of the trees which had been planted to form the enclosure.
An earthen mound, usually within an ornamental garden, on which a tree was planted.
Trees planted in an ornamental circle. For earthwork surrounding trees use TREE ENCLOSURE RING.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the extraction, processing & manufacture of finished goods. Includes structures associated with the supply, storage &/or transmission of power.
Horizontal tunnel opening from the surface used for haulage or access to a mine. It can also be used for drainage.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
Pit for mixing raw materials with water in the preparation of a clay body.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
An industrial manufacturing complex producing bricks.
An area where builders keep building materials such as brick, stone, planks and cement.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
A place from which chalk is extracted.
A place from which clay is extracted.
A pit used for the containment of clay whilst it is mixed to the right consistency for brickmaking.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
A steep-sided pit formed by, and for, the extraction of gravel.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.

A mill used for the production of mortar; a combination of sand, lime and water, used to make the joints between courses of bricks in buildings. In more recent times cement has replaced lime to create a quicker drying mortar.
A factory where rock gypsum is ground into a powder used in the production of plaster.
A site incorporating all of the production processes for the manufacture of plaster.
An excavation from which stone for building and other functions, is obtained by cutting, blasting, etc.
A place where gypsum is extracted.
A site where limestone is extracted.
A place where sandstone is excavated.
A place where shale, a laminated clay or silt which has been compressed by the weight of the rocks over it, is extracted from the ground.
A site where slate is quarried from the ground.
A pit from which sand is excavated.
A place where stone is dressed or shaped for use in building, etc.
A site used for the small scale extraction and working of surface boulders.
A complex, comprising a workshop and a storage yard, used by a stonemason.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A site used for all the processes associated with the manufacture of roof, floor or decorative tiles.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A mill for grinding or crushing bones, in the process of making bone china, for example.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.
A furnace for the manufacture of glass. Includes glass cones, open hearth and oil-fired furnaces.
A furnace for the calcining and roasting of a mixture of sand and fluxes as a preparatory stage in glass-making.
A site used for the production and/or working of glass.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A building or room where items of pottery are manufactured. Includes handcrafted and machine made pottery.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.
Chimney used on an industrial or commercial site.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
A horizontal tunnel dug specifically for draining, for example, a mine.
A building used to aid in the drying of goods, for example, by means of flowing air.
Surface workings including shallow shafts, lode workings, open-pit methods and quarrying including some mines of stone, clays, compounds, etc. See also MINERAL EXTRACTION SITE.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A bell-shaped pit used in early coal mining. Use with functional type if known, eg. COAL WORKINGS.
A site where coal is processed.
A site where copper ore is extracted directly from the surface of the ground.
The name of a class of excavations, found in chalk formations in England, consisting of a shaft sunk to the chalk, and there widening out into one or more chambers.
A pit for the extraction of fullers earth (a hydrous silicate of alumina), which was used for cleansing, and finishing, cloth and wool.
A site where iron ore is extracted.
A large pit formed by, and for, the extraction of iron ore.
A site where jet is extracted from the surface of the ground.
A place where lead ore is extracted from an open cast mine.
A ravine formed by using water to reveal or exploit a vein.
A pit from which marl, a mixture of clay and carbonate of lime, is excavated. Marl is used as a fertilizer.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.

Source from which stone utilized for the manufacture of non-flint artefacts, including axes, was obtained. Applied only to sources exploited during the Neolithic and earlier Bronze Age. Do not use for flint mining or knapping sites.
A site where tin ore is extracted from suspended fire waste in tin mine spoil heaps.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
A building or complex, housing powered machinery and employing a large workforce for manufacturing purposes. Use specific monument type where known.
A passageway, duct or pipe used for the conveyance of heat, gasses, smoke or air.

A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of beer and other alcoholic drinks. Size may range from a single room such as a microbrewery in a public house to a complex of buildings including production line machinery for bottling.
A factory concerned with the commercial manufacture of cider, as opposed to domestic production.
A room or small building kept at low temperatures for the storage of perishable items, particularly food.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
An establishment or works where the distilling of spirits is carried out.

A building where fish are stored. Often taking the form of a single storey building with one room, but also may provide living accommodation for a fisherman above. Found mainly in the South West of England.
A place where fish are processed after being caught.
A factory where flour was produced for use in food products.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A type of malt house.
A factory where fruit and seed oil is produced by an oil machine.
A building used to smoke fish or meat.
A sugar factory.
A site where sugar beet was processed before being washed and dried to form granulated sugar.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
Bleach works or bleach house for bleaching of textiles, etc.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of candles.
A site, often in a woodland clearing, used for the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
A works used for the production of copperas, a green iron sulphate which is used as a fixative in the dyeing process.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
An industrial complex concerned with the manufacture of gas for domestic use from coal and oil.
A place where graphite is extracted.
A site used for the manufacture of gunpowder.
A works where crude oil is distilled into its fractions or cuts.
A site where petroleum is drawn.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
A factory where paper is made. Use with power type where known.
A site where peat (vegetable matter decomposed in water and partly carbonised), used for fuel, is cut.
A structure used to dry peat on.
A fuel store for the storage of dried peat.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.
A mine from which potash is obtained. Potash is a deposit of potassium carbonate: the only example of a potash mine in the country is at Boulby in Cleveland.
Building housing the machinery for the shredding and grinding of wood in running water and pressing of the resulting fibres into a pulp.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A mine yielding rock salt.
A site, building or factory used for the production of salt.
A pit dug for the extraction of brine.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.
A site where tar is manufactured or combined with other substances to produce bitumen, for example.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of all types of wax.
A chamber in which minerals, metals, etc, are subjected to the continuous action of intense heat. Use specific type where known.
For reheating of worked metal or glass to make it malleable or to harden it after use for toolmaking, etc.
A furnace where metal is manufactured from ore.
Smelting furnace into which compressed hot air is driven.
A charcoal fired shaft furnace used for the direct reduction of iron ore to produce wrought iron.
An early form of lead furnace, set upon a hilltop or crest to utilize winds in smelting.
A small, open air bowl-shaped furnace, in which the flames are fanned by bellows. Used for both ferrous and non-ferrous smelting.
Large open hearth furnace often located inside a brick cone for use in steelmaking.
A furnace composed of two fire brick boxes: the fire was in the lower box and the upper box held the crucibles. Used in the manufacture of steel.
A furnace used for the refining of precious metals. eg. the separation of silver from argentiferous lead.
A furnace used for smelting or re-heating of iron, either for casting or for further working.
A furnace used for the smelting or reheating of lead.
A furnace for smelting ore in which the fuel and ore are mixed.
A reverberatory furnace used for forging wrought iron from pig iron using coal as fuel.
A furnace in which the flame is turned back over the substance to be heated.
A furnace constructed as a shaft with the fire at the bottom and the fuel and ore added from the top.
A hearth used for the reheating of metal slag to extract further metal.
A factory where glue is produced.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and equipment to and from the surface of a mine.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal horns.

A pit lined with the bony cores of animal horns. Thought to date from the 17th/18th centuries and believed to have been used in the tanning industry although some may have been used for casting cannon.
Any building designed or adapted to accommodate trades and manufacturing activity. Use more specific site where known.

An area of land owned by a developer, whether a private entrepreneur or a public authority, and divided into plots for leasing or sale to manufacturing or commercial concerns which may share some common services.
An area or defined space believed to have been used for trades and/or manufacturing activity. Only use when evidence for more specific site type is lacking.
A furnace or oven for burning, baking or drying. Use specific type where known.
A kiln for roasting ore.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.
A temporary kiln, in which the pots are stacked and baked in a pit underneath a bonfire.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A pit, sometimes found close to a church or cathedral, where bells were cast in medieval times.
A building containing a small stone cylindrical furnace, eg. used for tin smelting in Cornwall.
A place where boats are built and stored.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
Use only where evidence is specific, ie. copper/tin alloy. For working of copper based alloys of unknown composition use COPPER WORKING SITE.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
Building or structure covering a casting floor or pit.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A stone channel sunk into the ground, employed from the mid-19th century, to carry away gases produced during smelting.
A site where copper or copper based alloys are produced by smelting copper ore.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
Any factory or site using machine tools in a manufacturing or processing capacity.
A building or room used for any type of engineering work. Use more specific type where known.
A building or site where bloom iron or cast iron is forged into wrought iron.
Reheating of iron from a finery, for rolling or slitting.
A building used for the decarburizing of pig iron to produce wrought iron.
A workshop or factory for casting metals.
A workshop or factory where bells are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A workshop or factory where bronze articles are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A workshop or foundry where iron articles are made by casting molten material into moulds.
A pond used as a water supply for the operation of a furnace or blast furnace.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic iron.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic lead.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
A marker stone showing the extent of a measure of land containing a vein of ore.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A mill or works where needles were manufactured.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
Term for ore store/ore hopper, used particularly in Yorkshire and Derbyshire.
A stone-lined pit or tank, sometimes circular,  for concentrating ores by sedimentation.
Building or structure housing a buddle.
Where secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. LEAD MINE.
Where several minerals produced, use with other products and MINE, eg. ARSENIC MINE.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
Horse powered ore crusher, consisting of a stone wheel running over a circular iron or stone bed.
An area used for crushing mineral ore or stone. Often includes mechanically powered ore crushers.
A building containing mechanically powered ore crushers or rollers.
The place where metallic ores were crushed and washed to remove waste, forming a concentrate which could be used in a smelter.
A mill used for the sizing and drying of warp threads before they were wound onto warp beams as part of the power-weaving process.
A place where gold ore is extracted.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
A stone or platform on which lumps of ore are manually broken up.
Use with form of extraction where known. Also use MINE and other ores extracted where relevant, eg. SILVER MINE.
A place where manganese ore is extracted. Use with other ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
Also use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A pit dug in the prospect of finding valuable minerals, coal, metal ores, etc, beneath the ground surface.
Use with other minerals extracted and MINE where relevant, eg. ZINC MINE.
A manufacturing complex incorporating furnaces, calciner and condenser flues. Use SMELTERY for more modern type of plant.
A site where ores are smelted. Use more specific site type where known.
An ancilliary building within a larger works, as distinct from a SMELT MILL.
Building or structure housing a form of ore crushing device associated with tin mines.
A mine used for the extraction on tin bearing ore.
A crude, stone built structure, often roofless, used by tin miners to store equipment.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
A mine used for the extraction of tungsten bearing ore. Use with other mineral ores extracted and MINE, eg. TIN MINE.
A type of buddle used as an ore-cleaning device for seperating metallic ore from waste material by washing the dirty ore in a continuous flow of water.
Open-air area often terraced on which a range of ore processing operations are carried out.
A mine used for the extraction of zinc bearing ore. Use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where necessary, eg. LEAD MINE.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
A tower in which shot is made from molten lead poured through sieves at top and falling into water at bottom.
A site or building where silver was processed and/or worked and fashioned into objects.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A spoil heap consisting mainly of slag, pieces of refuse material separated from a metal during the smelting process.
A site where metal springs are manufactured.
A site containing plant and machinery for the manufacture of steel.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
Early form of powered hammer, usually wooden, used primarily in the iron industry.
A factory where metal wire is manufactured.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A factory used for processing raw materials. Use more specific mill type where known. See also TEXTILE MILL, for more narrow terms.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
A mill manufacturing bobbins for the textile industry.
A factory where buttons are manufactured.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.

A type of tower mill, either with turbine-type sails able to take wind from any direction, or with sails working with shrouds to direct wind from one direction. The sails directly drove millstones set beneath them.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
A mill in which sets of rollers were used to roll metal to set thicknesses or shapes such as rails, beams or rods.
A factory in which logs are converted to timber by running them through a series of saws.
A mill with machinery used to cut slabs of metal into rods, or thin sections, for use in nail making or wire drawing.
A factory where tobacco was ground to form snuff.
A steam-powered factory.
Any factory used for the manufacture of textiles.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
A factory where tapestries were manufactured.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.
A tower-like structure of wood or brick with a wooden cap and sails which are driven around by the wind producing power to work the internal machinery. Use with product type where known.
A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.
A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.
A windmill with a rotating cap containing the windshaft, and a stationary body in the form of a tower.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
An excavation made in the earth for the purpose of digging out metallic ores, coal, salt, or precious stones etc. Use specific type where known.
A mine in which access is gained by a straight entrance driven on a constant downward slope. Use with product(s) extracted and MINE where known, eg. COAL MINE.

A site where flint seams within chalk have been exploited by digging deep vertical shafts, often with horizontal galleries radiating out from the base. Use for Neolithic examples and for Post Medieval gunflint industry.
A building found at the site of a mine. Use specific type where known.
A vertical or inclined excavation giving access to an underground mine.
A building housing a boiler, often connected to a steam engine house.
A type of engine house creating power by means of compressed air, typically associated with collieries where it is used for raising coal.
Wooden or ferro-concrete tower for cooling waste, hot water from a power station. The water cascades from the top of the tower to a pond in the bottom.
A treadwheel using a donkey as motive power. Usually found operating wells.
Building containing transformers to reduce the high voltage of the National Grid to the lower voltage of domestic supply.
A machine, powered by steam, gas, electricity or other energy source, which produces energy of movement. Use for stationary industrial engines rather than transport use.
An engine in which the mechanical force of steam is made available as a motive power for driving machinery.
A rotary prime mover. Turbines may be steam, water or gas operated.
A simple wind-driven machine used for a variety of purposes.
A building housing an engine. Use specific type where known.
A building housing a beam engine.
A building housing a turbine.
Expanding storage tank for gas, often includes a meter for measuring the amount used.
A simple machine, worked by horses, to provide a power take-off for driving agricultural machinery.
A horse-powered winding engine used at mining sites.
Large piston used to operate lifting bridges, lock gates, etc.
A building or set of buildings and structures where power, especially electrical or mechanical, is generated. Use more specific type where known.
A waterworks pumping station.
A pumping station used in the production of hydraulic power, eg. in warehouse complexes, goods depots on railways, etc.
A steam-powered machine used for raising ore or water from a mine.
A device for converting one voltage of alternating current to another voltage.
The line of a flat rod system transmitting power from an engine or waterwheel.
A structure associated with forges, watermills, water-powered factories, etc.
The rectangular pit in which the lower part of a waterwheel revolves.
A building to house waterwheels, attached to a WATERMILL or water-powered factory.
A building housing a whim, a machine worked by a horse, used for raising ores, etc, from a mine.
A mechanical structure, consisting of a roller or beam on supports, round which a rope or chain is wound, and used for various purposes, eg. raising a bucket from a well, etc.
Form of dam, usually associated with ponds supplying water for blast furnaces.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.
Pit for the depostion of ore sediment from waste water collected from ore washing.
A large tank where particles suspended in water, or other liquids, are allowed to sink to the bottom forming a sediment.
A conical or flat-topped tip of waste discarded from a mine or similar site.
Pit for soaking animal hides as part of the tanning process.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A site where rough stone is processed, shaped, worked or formed into finished products.
A site where artefacts are manufactured from jet.
A site where millstones have been cut to shape and/or fabricated from smaller pieces of stone.
A site used for the manufacture and finishing of querns.
A site or building used for processing shale. Shale can be fashioned into goods or, if bituminous, distilled to produce oil, naphtha or tar.
A place where shoes and boots are mended.
Place where tanned leather is dressed and coloured.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A site used for the manufacture of leather products.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
A manufacturing complex where the hides of animals are turned into leather, consisting of buildings for fleecing and drying, as well as treatment pits.
A pit or tank containing chemicals for the preserving of animal hide.
Large field or yard used to lay fabrics out ready for bleaching.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
Large wooden hammer beams pounding cloth in a fulling solution.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
A factory where lace is manufactured.

A very long, narrow, roofed building, often two-storeyed, used for the manufacture of rope. Often attached to warehousing, an engine house or offices. Can be included within the complex of a textile mill.
A place where sails are manufactured.
Field or area of ground where washed new cloth is stretched out to dry.
Building for testing the condition and strength of textiles.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A barrel-making workshop or factory, found in conjunction with a number of industries.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.
A place where tree trunks were sawn into planks by hand.
