Pond for storing cut lengths of timber to prevent them becoming seasoned.
A building where timber was allowed to dry and harden, to render it fit for use as a working material.
An open yard or place where timber is stacked or stored.
A place where wheels and wheeled vehicles were manufactured, originally from wood.
Used for boiling sections of willow for basket making, etc.
A place where tobacco is made into cigarettes, cigars, etc.
A factory that manufactures toys.
Usually a complex of buildings for the processing of raw materials. Use specific type where known.
A building or room used for small scale manufacture. Use more specific term where possible.

Sites, building, structures & features associated with the construction, maintenance & supply of maritime craft. Includes associated ancillary structures such as navigation aids, dockyards, wharves, etc; does not include vessels.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
A structure which protects a beach or harbour by breaking the force of the waves.
A beacon used for coastal navigation. Many date from the Medieval period.
An office, particularly at a seaport, at which customs are collected.
An artificial area of open water, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
A sheltered port for ships.
A mole or pier-like structure situated at the entrance of a harbour, or running out into a lake or the sea, usually used for the landing of craft.
A platform, sometimes floating, for the landing of passengers and goods from vessels.
A building designed to house a lifeboat, usually with a stone ramp to launch the boat into the sea.
A massive structure, usually of stone, serving as a pier or breakwater, or joining two places separated by water.
A post to which ropes are attached to secure vessels at a landing place.
A structure of iron or wood, open below, running out into the sea and used as a promenade and landing stage.
A settlement area that combines a harbour and terminal facilities at the interface between land and water transportation systems.
An artificial paved bank or solid landing place built parallel to, or projecting out from, the shoreline to serve in the loading and unloading of vessels.
Non-military maritime flood and erosion defences.
A conspicuous object, such as a beacon, used by mariners to aid navigation at sea.
A structure inclined towards the water on which a ship may be built or lowered into the water.
A waterside depot for coals brought from the collieries for shipment, furnished with staging and chutes for loading vessels.
A large wooden structure built alongside the water's edge where ships may lie for unloading.
A large disc of stone revolving on an axis, used for grinding, sharpening and polishing.
One of a pair of large circular stones used for grinding corn in a mill.
Use more specific term where known.

A perforated stone basin usually built into the wall of a church on the south side of the altar. Used for carrying away the ablutions (wine and water used to rinse the chalice, and wash the priests hands after communion).

Traditionally, dating from the medieval period, this was an area on the north bank of the Thames where the Merchants of the Hanse conducted their business. Now includes a similar establishment in a provincial town.
A long seat, usually made of stone or wood, with or without a back.
The unarticulated remains of the body of a human being. If articulated use inhumation.
Fixed instrument to measure altitude of stars and planets.

A structure used to show the time of day by means of the sun shining on a 'gnomon', the shadow of which falls on the surface of the dial which is marked with a diagram showing the hours. Can be freestanding, usually on a pillar, or fixed to a building.
A vane usually combined with crossed rods to show the four compass points. Used to indicate the direction of the wind.
An ornamental, commemorative tablet. Use with materials field when indexing.
A large stone used by cattle to rub up against and so scratch themselves.
A garden ornament, usually of stone or metal, designed in the the form of a vase used to receive the ashes of the dead.
A large, decorative garden ornament resembling a vase.
A large mounted gun, now disused and placed in a prominent position as a piece of street furniture or as a feature.""
A site where the baiting of animals took place. Use more specific site type where known.
A site used for the sport of badger baiting using fighting dogs.
A pit where bears were housed for baiting and entertainment purposes. If not used for baiting use BEAR ENCLOSURE.
An arena for bull-baiting, not a tethering ring.
A pit or enclosed area used for cockfighting.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
A closely mown piece of ground used for the game of lawn bowling.
A building or room in which images of outside objects are projected on to a screen from a long-focus lens using natural light.
A building where people pay to see films and 'moving pictures'.
A building occupied by a club or commonly used for club activities.
A club founded to provide education, relaxation, and recreation for working men.
An establishment where musical performances take place.
A wall and area of ground where the game of fives is played.
A prepared area of ground used to play the game of golf on.
The principal stand at a sporting ground, eg. at a racecourse.
A hall licensed for musical performances, singing, dancing and other entertainments, exclusive of dramatic performance.
An often ornately decorated theatre for the performance of opera.
A Cornish Medieval amphitheatre used for the performance of mystery plays and sports.
An object supported by a crosspiece on a post, used by knights as a target in tilting.
A piece of ground on which athletes race.
An area or route marked out for the site of a race.
A piece of ground used for motor racing.
A public ground with facilities for games and other activities.
A building, usually at a sports ground, with facilities for players and spectators.
A large, manmade pool, usually lined with tiles, rubber or similar. Can be placed in the open air, eg. a LIDO, or built as part of a covered sports centre.
A prepared area, traditionally grass, where tennis is played.
A building used primarily for the performing of plays.
An elevated table or podium on which to place or sacrifice offerings to the deities.
A tomb or memorial, resembling an altar, often with a recumbent effigy on top.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious man or monk, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of banks, ditches, stones, timber posts or trees which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments. Use specific type where known.
An area of a church, often a free-standing building, in which baptism is administered
A tower or turret in which bells are hung.
A representation of the crucifixion of Christ or related scenes as a sculpture in a churchyard, etc.
A freestanding building, or a room or recess serving as a place of Christian worship in a church or other building. Use more specific type where known.
A chapel built into the structure of a bridge.
A chapel built on, or at the end of, a causeway.
A chapel attached to, or inside, a church, endowed for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.
A chapel attached to or founded by a college.
Use both terms.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.
The building attached to a cathedral or collegiate church where the dean, prebendaries or monks and canons met for the transaction of business.
The principal church of a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
An enclosed area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
An area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
A Neolithic monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by frequent causeways, and often accompanied by an internal bank, also causewayed.

A monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by several causeways, surrounding a central circular area used for funerary activities, often concealed originally beneath an earthen mound. Index with barrow type where known.
A building used for public Christian worship. Use more specific type where known.
A church attached to or founded by a college.
The foremost church within a parish.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
A stone found on route to a churchyard on which the coffin is rested during transportation.
A communal residence of secular priests and/or other clerics sometimes with the condition of learning and education attached.
A free-standing structure, in the form of a cross (+), symbolizing the structure on which Jesus Christ was crucified and sacred to the Christian faith. Use specific type where known.
A sculpted cross, or a cross incised into stone or trees, to mark a parish boundary.
Use both terms.
A cross found in a market place.
A cross, erected on a highway or in an open place, at which monks and others used to preach.
A cross erected within a town, usually funded by the inhabitants.
A cross erected in a village.
A stone with a cross carved into the surface.

A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions surrounded by a concentric arrangement of annular or pennanular grooves. More complex designs may also occur.
A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions, generally created by chipping or pecking.

A long narrow rectangular earthwork enclosure of Neolithic date, usually defined by a bank and ditch and presumed to be of ceremonial function. Known examples range in length from less than 100m to c.10km.
A vessel, usually made of stone, which contains the consecrated water for baptism. Use a broader monument type if possible.
Site types normally or frequently associated with burials which in some instances may have had solely religious or ritual functions.
Artificial mound of earth, turf and/or stone, normally constructed to contain or conceal burials. Use specific type where known.

A poorly understood Neolithic monument comprising a very long, narrow earthen mound. They may be of single-phase construction, or represent the addition of a linear extension to the bank of an existing Long Barrow.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within an earthen mound. Use more precise term where known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
Not a round barrow ploughed out at one end, but a specific type, the flat edge being additionally defined by stone slabs.

A rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound of Neolithic date, usually accompanied by flanking or encircling ditches, and normally associated with human remains. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
A form of Neolithic long barrow comprising an oval, rather than rectangular or trapezoidal mound.
A monument featuring an artificial circular shallow depression surrounded by a bank which runs around the rim of the depression.
A circular bank surrounding an area where burials were placed.

Hemispherical mound surrounded by a ditch (or occasionally two or more concentric ditches), often accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank. Mound and ditch may sometimes be separated by a berm. Use specific type where known.
A round barrow in which the mound and ditch are separated from each other by a berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
A round barrow featuring a mound surrounded by a ditch, with no intervening berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external bank.
A collective term applied to Bronze Age round barrows displaying more complex external morphology than the simple bowl barrow. Use appropriate specific term.
A form of round barrow intermediate between the Bell Barrow and the Disc Barrow. Only use where it is not possible to determine specific type.
A round barrow featuring a small mound separated from a ditch of much greater diameter by a wide berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
A round barrow featuring a low, wide mound surrounded by a ditch which may be accompanied by an external bank.
A burial monument, usually of Iron age date, comprising a small square ditched enclosure surrounding a central interment, which may also have been covered by a mound.
An interment of human or animal remains. Use specific type where known. If component use with wider site type. Use FUNERARY SITE for optimum retrieval in searches.
Deliberate interment of a complete, or substantially complete, animal. Use the object type thesaurus term ANIMAL REMAINS where skeleton is fragmentary.
A body which has been interred in boggy or marshy ground or other similarly waterlogged environment. Interment may have been deliberate or accidental.
A high status Iron Age grave in which a two or four wheeled vehicle accompanies a frequently richly furnished inhumation burial. A barrow may overlie the grave.

Inhumation rite in which charcoal is included with the buried corpse, possibly in an attempt to preserve the body. Thought to be associated with high status burials of the early medieval and medieval period.

A funeral rite in which the human body is burnt, usually on a pyre, leaving fragmentary charred or completely combusted remains. Often found buried, occasionally in a container associated with grave goods.
Urn containing a cremation. Where component use with wider site type.
An inhumation burial in which the body is covered by a shroud, placed in a coffin of stone, wood or lead and covered with gypsum, plaster or lime. Roman and early Medieval.
An interment of unburnt, articulated human remains. Use specific type where known.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with the knees brought up against the chest. This is a more extreme form of crouched inhumation.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of more than 90 degrees.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is laid out in an approximately straight line, whether face up, face down, or on its side.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of less than 90 degrees.
A burial in which the body is placed in, or covered by a boat, which is then covered with earth. Use with barrow type where relevant.
An inhumation, usually Roman, which has been covered by tiles to form a tent-like structure over the body; the apex is covered by ridge tiles.
A place where dead bodies are buried together. Often unconsecrated ground.
A pit over which a  corpse has been cremated on a pyre into which the remains and debris, and sometime grave goods, collapse and are buried. Generally confined to the Roman period.
A deep pit used for the burial of plague victims.

A built structure, generally below ground, designed for the interment of several burials over a period of time. Usually constructed with a door or sealed entrance to allow reopening for further burials.
A burial vault built to contain the remains of members of a single family, household or dynasty.
A stony mound containing or concealing deliberately deposited human remains. Use specific type where known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of stones. Use more precise term where known.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.

A rectangular or trapezoidal non-megalithic stony mound of Neolithic date, with human remains in cists rather than a large chamber. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
A low, wide, circular ring or bank of stones surrounding an open, roughly circular area which is (or was initially) free of cairn material. The inner and outer faces of the bank may be kerbed.
A roughly hemispherical mound constructed primarily of stones, normally containing or covering one or more human burials. The mound may be surrounded and partly retained by a low stone kerb.
A roughly square mound of stones which may also contain or conceal a burial.
A circular bank of stones and turf, sometimes accompanied by a ditch, surrounding a natural outcrop of rock, usually a tor, or an earthfast boulder.
An area of ground, set apart for the burial of the dead.
A cluster of closely spaced barrows and related monuments (eg. ring ditches). Use with specific barrow-types where known.
A group of cairns in close proximity which are predominantly funerary or ritual in nature.
A cemetery comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels.

A cemetery of later prehistoric date comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels. The cemetery area is partly or wholly surrounded by an earthwork bank and/or ditch.
A village cemetery where cinerary urns were buried in large numbers during the Bronze Age.

An area used for the deposition of human remains where the principal funeral rite is the burial of the corpse complete. Generally indicated by the discovery of articulated human skeletal remains, occasionally with evidence of coffins and/or grave goods.
An area of ground belonging to a church, often used as a burial ground.
A cemetery comprising inhumations or cremations interred in stone cists.
A place of burial for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of earth or stone. Use more specific type where known.

A form of Neolithic burial monument primarily found in Cornwall and the Scilly Isles. It comprises a round cairn, usually with a retaining wall or kerb, and an entrance leading directly into a chamber.
Neolithic chambered tomb featuring a passage with lateral and/or end chambers.
Use appropriate type.
A form of Neolithic burial monument comprising a large circular stone or earthen mound, with a low and narrow entrance passage leading to a wider and higher stone built chamber.
A megalithic tomb of Neolithic date comprising a chamber bounded by large upright orthostats, often only three or four in number, which support a large capstone.
A building where the bones of the dead were stored.

Generally rectangular structure normally used for burial purposes, and formed from stone slabs set on edge, and covered by one or more horizontal slabs or capstones. Cists may be built on the surface or sunk into the ground.
A grave lined with slabs of stone or slate and covered by a large slab of stone. Commonly found on the Isle of Man.
A chest made of stone, wood or lead, used to enclose a dead body.
A stone coffin embellished with sculpture.
A prehistoric coffin made out of a hollow tree trunk.
A wall with niches in a CREMATORIUM to display the urns containing ashes. Use only when related to funerary site.
A building or site where bodies are burnt, and the ashes collected for burial or dispersal.
A vault, often located under a chancel or chancel aisle, containing an altar and usually used for burial.
A place of burial. Use more specific type where known.
A stone used to cover a grave.
A slab of stone, either standing or recumbent, inscribed with a cross. Usually found in association with burials.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance of a tomb.
A small Anglo-Saxon cross-slab buried on the breast or beneath the head of a corpse. The term can also apply to a stone placed beneath the head of some prehistoric burials.
A North country memorial imitating a wattled hut decorated with formalized bears or snakes.
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.
A monumental burial place, usually for a single person or family.
A building or room used for holding, viewing, identifying or examining dead bodies prior to burial or cremation.

A subrectangular earthen enclosure defined by a ditch, usually with an internal bank, assumed to have been used for the primary exposure or burial of human remains in the Neolithic period prior to secondary burial elsewhere.
Timber or stone built structure, traces of which are found within some long and round barrows, in which human remains were interred prior to mound construction.
A building, site or container used to store the bones of the dead after they have been removed from graves to allow new burials.
A grave or sepulchre including a monument. Use specific type where known.
A tomb designed in the form of a cist or stone box placed over a burial. Its outward form often reproduces the features of the classical sarcophagus or medieval effigy base.
A type of tomb in the form of a slab raised on freestanding legs.
A horizontal stone placed across a grave.

Circular or sub-circular enclosure defined by a bank and (usually internal) ditch, with one or two (rarely more) entrances. Of ceremonial/ritual function, they contain a variety of internal features including timber or stone circles.
A late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age earthwork enclosure distinguished from a henge primarily by its larger size, irregular shape, and greater complexity of internal features.

A small, circular Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age enclosure which bears a morphological resemblance to henges, but may belong to another category of circular earthwork-defined monuments, or is enclosed by something other than a bank and ditch.
A small hut, dwelling or cave, usually in a secluded spot, in which a hermit lived. Hermits chose to live solitary lives often due to religious motives.
An early Medieval commemorative monument in the form of a stone which has been inscribed with symbols.
A Prehistoric monument type in South West England in which a natural boulder is surrounded by a man-made kerb of stones.
A covered gateway, at the entrance to a churchyard, where during a funeral a coffin could be set down until the vicar arrived.
A high pole, painted with spiral stripes of different colours and decked with flowers, erected on an open space, often the village green, for merrymakers to dance around on May Day.
A labyrinthine garden feature, common during the 16th and 17th centuries, created by cutting shallow pathways into deep lawns.

A place of worship for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers. The Religious Society of Friends is a denomination founded by George Fox in c.1650 who believed in passivist principles and a rejection of the sacrament.

A complex of buildings, often within an enclosure, housing a pre-Benedictine Reform secular religious community. Now commonly used to describe the main church within such a complex, which over time attained higher status.
A mound in excess of 150 metres in diameter, of Late Neolithic date and presumed ritual function, eg. Silbury Hill.
A Muslim temple or place of worship.
Upright stones engraved on the edges with a Celtic script consisting of lines or notches.

An enclosure of Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age date, related to henges, defined by a circular arrangement of pits, probably none of which originally held posts. More than one circle, concentrically arranged, may be present.
A small, ornate structure in which candles were placed either during masses for the dead or to indicate the position of the cemetery at night .
A large, circular hollow, often with a platform and seating built into the sides, used for preaching.
A wall enclosing a precinct.
A hiding place for a (Roman Catholic) priest.
A stone or boulder which lies lengthways on the ground and may be used as a table, altar etc. Use only for isolated stones.
Use only for a monastic house of unknown status, religious order and uncertain authenticity.
A religious house governed by an abbot or abbess. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A subsidiary form of preceptory provided with a chapel. Use specific type where known.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Hospitallers for administrative purposes on their estates.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Templars for administrative purposes on their estates.
A monastic enclave dependent on a mother house.
A small monastery or nunnery of the Augustinian order dependent on a larger mother house.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on an English mother house.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on an English mother house.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cluniac order dependent on an English mother house.
A residence of two or three monks of the Gilbertine order dependent on an English mother house.
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on an English mother house.
Subsidiary settlement of lay brothers attached to some Carthusian monasteries.
Mixed house of nuns and religious men.
A mixed house of Augustinian nuns, canonesses and canons.
A mixed house of nuns and religious men of the Benedictine order.
An abbey of the Bridgettine double order of nuns and religious men.
A priory of double order of Fontevrault nuns and brethren.
A priory of Gilbertine double order of nuns and canons.
Houses specifically for men and of chiefly mendicant religious orders. The status of priory is represented in several friaries. Use with PRIORY if required.
A house of friars, originally hermits from Mount Carmel. Also known as ' white friars'.
A house of friars of the order of St Dominic. Also known as Friars Preachers or 'Black Friars'.
A friary belonging to the Franciscan order. Includes houses of both Friars Minor and Friars Observant or Capuchins.
A friary belonging to the Crutched Friars also known as Crosiers or Fratres.

TERM: FRIARY OF FRIARS OF THE SACK
SCOPE_NOTE: A friary belonging to the Friars of the Sack also known as Friars of Penance or Penitentia.
A friary belonging to the Pied Friars also known as Friars of Blessed Mary or St Mary de Arens.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Augustinian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Benedictine order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Carthusian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cistercian order.
Houses specifically of monks, canons or religious men but not friars.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canons.
An abbey or priory for monks of the Benedictine order.
A residence of the Bonhommes brethren, who followed the Augustinian rule.
An abbey or priory of Carthusian monks.
An abbey or priory of Cistercian monks.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac monks.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine monks.
An abbey or priory of Grandmontine monks.
An abbey or priory of Premonstratensian canons.
An abbey or priory of Savigniac monks. Order merged with Cistercians c1147.
An abbey or priory belonging to the Tironian order.
An abbey or priory of the Trinitarian brethren also named Maturins.
Houses specifically of nuns/canonesses or religious women.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canonesses.
An abbey or priory for nuns ofthe Benedictine order.
An abbey or a priory of Cistercian nuns.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac nuns.
An abbey or priory of Dominican nuns.
An abbey of Franciscan nuns also known as Minoresses or Poor Clares.
A priory of Premonstratensian canonesses.
A priory of the female Order of Knights Hospitallers.
A manor or estate owned and run by an order of knights and governed by a preceptor.
An estate or manor of a subordinate community of the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem. Includes the mother house, the Priory of St. John, Clerkenwell.

The residence of a preceptor, officials and servants, etc, supervising the estates of the Knights Templars military order. Includes the mother house styled the Temple, London. The Order was suppressed in 1312.
A monastery governed by a prior or prioress. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, FRIARY, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A pit which appears to have been dug for, or which contains, objects apparently deposited for reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction. Index with principal object types.

A shaft which appears to have been dug for, or which contains objects apparently deposited for, reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction (eg. of stone, water, etc). Index with principal object types.

A decorative design or illustration, often an anthropomorphic or geometrical image, carved into a stone surface, such as a cave wall or free-standing stone. Usually, though not always, of Prehistoric date.
A stone on which Runes have been inscribed. Often used as memorials though not always associated with a burial.
A sacred area of a building or a consecrated piece of land.
A small carved figure, usually female in appearance, probably representing  fertility charms, found on Romanesque churches in the West of England, eg. Kilpeck.
A place where worship is offered or devotions are paid to a deity or saint.
A stone or boulder which has been deliberately set upright in the ground. Use only for isolated stones. Otherwise use specific type where known.

A monument within a church or cathedral representing one of the stations of the cross. Usually images or pictures of successive incidents of the Passion, they are intended to be visited for meditation and prayer.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.
A single line, or two or more roughly parallel lines, of standing stones set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of standing stones, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
An approximately circular or oval setting of spaced, usually freestanding, upright stones. More than one circle may be present, arranged concentrically.
A circular arrangement of spaced stone uprights set within a high bank, often interrupted by a formal entrance gap.

A stone circle featuring four upright stones standing at the corners of an irregular quadrilateral. The monument may feature more than 4 stones, overall, but the corner stones are often the most prominent.
A stone circle featuring a stone which lies lengthways between two of the upright standing stones.
An arrangement of one or more standing stones. Use particularly for isolated recumbent stones, or where original form of monument unclear. Use specific type where known.
A place of worship for Jewish people.
Use for places of worship. For later landscape features use, eg. GARDEN TEMPLE.
A Roman sanctuary, devoted to the Graeco-Roman cult of Mithras.

Approximately circular or oval setting of spaced post holes indicating the former presence of a free-standing arrangement of upright timber posts. Often regarded as a wooden equivalent of the better known stone circles.
A shaft or pit dug in the ground over a supply of spring-water.

A well or spring, possessing religious or otherwise ritualistic significance, around which a structure, such as a niche, wall or shelter, has been constructed. In the case of the water source being a natural spring, double-index with SPRING.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the conveyance of goods &/or passengers.  Includes man-made routeways, mechanical structures & some vehicle types where it is deemed necessary to record such as monuments.
A system of overhead cables from which cars or containers are suspended (usually driven electrically).
A building at an airport from where passengers embark and disembark from an aircraft.
An aircraft, either whole or in part. Aircraft often survive as commemorative monuments, gate guardians or crash sites.
An area or site used for the landing and take-off of aircraft, often including associated buildings, equipment and other installations.
A site, including an airfield and customs house, where air passengers embark and disembark.
A large shed for the housing of aircraft, etc.
A structure used for the housing and servicing of aircraft.
A hangar for the storage and maintenance of dirigible motor-driven balloons.
A structure of wood, stone, iron, brick or concrete, etc, with one or more intervals under it to span a river or other space. Use specific type where known.
A bridge over a canal.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
A movable bridge lifted at one end by chains or ropes either to stop traffic passing over it or to let traffic pass under it.
A bridge that incorporates a span that moves upwards vertically to provide a passageway for navigation.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A bridge whose deck is hung from above by large cables, chains or pinned iron or steel bars hanging from towers.
A movable bridge that swings or rotates around a central pier, or one that is pivoted only at one end, to provide a passageway for navigation.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
A large, metal or wooden structure, used for raising, lowering and moving heavy objects. Use more specific type where known.
A stone, situated alongside a road, providing directions to travellers.
A prepared slope on which rails are laid to enable early tramroads and railways to negotiate a steep gradient.
A structure consisting of a box or platform for carrying goods or passengers from one level to another. Use specific type where known.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, set up on a road, canal or railway to mark the miles from or to a place.
A stone set up on a road or path to mark the miles from or to a place.
A building used to house railway engines.
A building in which railway wagons can unload local goods.
A site where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.
A controlled point with warning lights and gates or barriers where a road crosses a railway line.
A line or track consisting of iron or steel rails, on which passenger carriages or goods wagons are moved, usually by a locomotive engine.
A railway worked by the propulsive force of compressed air or by the formation of a vacuum.

A railway, usually by the sea, linking the beach with the cliff top. Various mechanisms were used the most common being that the cars were attached to a cable and winding drum and were balanced so that one travelled up, as the other came down.
A structure with semaphore arms and/or coloured lights used as a means of warning on railway systems.
Use both terms.
A place where railway trains regularly stop for taking up and setting down passengers or for receiving goods for transport.
A tunnel running under a river or a hillside through which a railway line runs.
A piece of machinery on which a railway engine, carriage or wagon can be rotated at a railway terminal.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a railway across low-lying land or water.
A place where trams are maintained and refitted, etc.
A track inlaid into a surface, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers and/or goods or raw materials.
A track consisting of flanged strips used in early colliery railways.

A building, with adjacent open areas, in which buses are maintained, usually having an extensive area free from upright columns or stanchions to permit overnight storage, repair bays, stores and an office.
A structure providing protection against the weather at bus stops.
An outbuilding used for the storage and maintenance of horse-drawn carriages.
A building used for housing, and protecting from the weather, carts, waggons and farm implements, often open-fronted.
An outbuilding where a horse-drawn carriage is kept.
A shallow place in a river or other stretch of water, where people, animals and vehicles may cross.
A block for mounting a horse.
A way between different places, used by horses, travellers on foot and vehicles.
A passageway or lane between buildings.
A road or track specifically used by drovers or herders to drive their animals to market.
A way, path or road through a cutting.
Narrow, rough tracks often over upland routes used by packhorse trains to carry goods.
A road whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A pathway, not necessarily designed as such, beaten down by the feet of travellers.
A road or pathway raised above surrounding low, wet or uneven ground.
A path for pedestrians only.
A road or way along a ridge of downs or low range of hills.
A tunnel running under a river or through a hill along which vehicles may travel.
Stones placed in the bed of a stream or on wet ground, to enable crossing on foot.
A series of flat-topped structures, usually made of stone or wood, used to facilitate a person's movement from one level to another.
A set of steps or a framework of bars and steps for crossing over a fence or wall.
A track inlaid into the road surface of a street or road, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers.

A structure consisting of three stretches of tramline joined by points. The tram is able to go forward, reverse and then go forward again changing line each time until it has turned around completely.
A marker, of stone, wood or metal, used to delineate the limits of a stretch of highway, river or canal subject to a toll charge.
A gate on a toll road where travellers had to pay a toll to the toll-keeper.
A post bearing one or more signs indicating the direction, and often the distance, to specified locations or routes.
A bridge, usually resting on a series of arches, carrying roadways or railways over low-lying areas.
A structure used for the lifting of boats and other water craft.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.

An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves and warehouses, where barges, narrow boats and other canal vessels can load and unload goods and supplies.
A place where canal boats are built and maintained.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a canal, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
An enclosure containing a dock, boat yard, warehouse, etc, in which canal vessels are built and repaired, and all sorts of stores and merchandise for transportation brought together.
A channel which feeds water from a reservoir into a canal when the water level gets low.
A massive structure designed to transfer canal boats between different canal or river navigations, eg. Anderton boat lift.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A supply of water used to keep canals that were vulnerable to water shortage topped up.
A channel for taking a rapidly flowing stream of water away from a canal lock, or away from the canal itself.
A tunnel with a canal running through it.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a river, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A river canalized for shipping.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a river where boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods and passengers.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land, both natural & man-made, which cannot be assigned to a particular class (for example, railings).

A structure over an opening usually formed of wedge-shaped blocks of brick or stone held together by mutual pressure and supported at the sides; they can also be formed from moulded concrete/ cast metal. A component; use for free-standing structure only.
A trench dug to contain a sill beam, a horizontal timber beam used as a foundation for the wall of a building. Use wider site type where known.
Use for free standing column.
A layer of stone, brick or boards, etc, on which people tread. Use broader site type where known.
A picture or pattern produced by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours. May be in the form of a floor.
A path or road for pedestrians, laid or beaten in with stones or other materials.
Component: Use wider site type where known.
A painting executed directly onto a wall.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mine or bombshell.
The limit to an area as defined on a map or by a marker of some form, eg. BOUNDARY WALL. Use specific type where known.
An earthen bank that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A cairn used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A marker of some form used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
An earthwork used as a boundary marker.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, used to indicate the limit of an area or piece of land.
A stone or metal post that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
A stone that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
Any wall enclosing a building or complex of buildings, eg. prisons, dockyards, factories, etc, or to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A construction of wood or metal used to enclose an area of land, a building, etc.
Usually a row of bushes or small trees planted closely together to form a boundary between pieces of land or at the sides of a road.
A fence or barrier made of metal or wooden rails.
A structure with a roof to provide shelter from the weather for occupants or contents. Use specific type where known.

A site where a building once stood as identified by a level area of ground, often compacted or made from man-made materials. Use only where specific function is unknown, otherwise use more specific term.
A detached subordinate building. Use specific type where known, eg. DAIRY.
Component. Use wider site type where known.
A room or group of rooms usually below the ground level and usually under a building, often used for storing fuel, provisions or wines.
A covered walk, walled on one side and usually arcaded on the other, surrounding or partly surrounding an open area in a monastery or similar complex of Christian buildings.
A building or room, purpose built for the teaching, rehearsing and playing of music.
A vault or crypt under a church or chapel. Use wider site type where known.
An underground room or building with an arched roof, often used as a burial chamber. Use wider site type where known.
A stone (including standing stones, natural boulders and rock outcrops) decorated with carved motifs.
A carved figure or design.
A tower built to display a large clock.
A building used to store coal.
A long and narrow hollow or trench dug in the ground, often used to carry water though it may be dry for much of the year.
A bank or mound of earth used as a rampart or fortification.
Earthworks of uncertain date and purpose, consisting of cross-shaped banks sometimes with an accompanying ditch. Their distribution is largely confined to North Yorkshire.
An area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or other similar barrier. Use specific type where known.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the boundary follows an irregular curving course.
A circular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
An area of land, in the shape of a D, enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
An oval shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.

A site consisting of, usually two, sub-circular enclosures linked by a linear ditch running tangentially to the enclosure boundaries. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period in the Wessex region.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows a circular course, but is not regularly laid out.
An area of land enclosed by one or several boundary ditches. Double index with a term to indicate the shape of the enclosure where known.
An area of land enclosed by two parallel ditches. Use with specific shaped enclosure where known.
An enclosure where the boundary consists of a line of discrete pits, as opposed to a continuous ditch. Use with a term that describes the shape of the monument.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier consists of several straight or near straight sections.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a polygon and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A rectangular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.

A square shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier. Small square enclosures (with sides of less than c.20m) have been interpreted as the remains of square barrows of Iron Age date.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a trapezoid and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of flint artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context.
A place where material used for burning is stored.
A movable stucture which enables or prevents entrance to be gained. Usually situated in a wall or similar barrier and supported by gate posts.
A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.
Casual scribbles or pictographs on ancient walls, stones or other surfaces. In more recent times applied to humourous, satiric or obscene writings or drawings executed anonymously in public places.
The slab or place on which a fire is made.
A mechanical lift or elevator, used to lift goods, etc.
A hollow, concave formation or place, which has sometimes been dug out.
An area of land which has been drained or cleared for habitation and/or cultivation.
A length of straight, curved or angled earthwork or cropmark of uncertain date or function.
A complex or network of earthwork or cropmark linear ditches, banks or other features. Use specific type where known.
Area feature visible as an earthwork or cropmark with no known function.
A cairn erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
A natural or artificial elevation of earth or stones, such as the earth heaped upon a grave. Use more specific type where known.
Use only for natural features mistakenly assumed to be archaeological or natural features with archaeological significance.
A subterranean feature entered from a hillside, cliff face, etc. A cave may have been used for occupation, storage, burial, refuse, or as a hide-away. Index with site type or objects where known.

Soil marks and other features of natural origin, including periglacial frost wedging, solifluction deposits, abandoned water courses, etc, recorded to avoid future confusion with features of human origin.
A point where water issues naturally from the rock or soil onto the ground or into a body of surface water.
Use only where stone is natural or where there is no indication of function.
A forest killed by rising sea-level. Nowadays only tree stumps survive.
A channel used for or formed by the conveyance of water. Can be natural, eg. a river or artificial eg. an aqueduct. Use more specific type where known.
A brick, stone or iron receptacle for baking bread or other food in.
A conduit or pipes, used primarily for conveying petroleum from oil wells to a refinery, or for supplying water to a town or district, etc.
A hole or cavity in the ground, either natural or the result of excavation. Use more specific type where known.
A single line, or pair of roughly parallel lines, of pits set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes. The pits are not thought to have held posts.
A spatially discrete group of pits usually containing artefactual material with little or no accompanying evidence for structural features.
Unspecified. Use specific type where known.
A levelled area of ground, circular in shape, used as the base on which a monument was built.Sometimes raised, a platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a monument.
A hole dug to provide a firm base for an upright post, often with stone packing. Use broader monument type where known.
An inclined plane connecting two different levels, used to accomodate the movement of vehicles, wheeled apparatus,livestock etc.
A communal dining room, especially in schools, colleges and monasteries.
A wall or masonry construction built for the purpose of retaining or supporting a bank of earth, wall, rampart etc.

Circular or near circular ditches, usually seen as cropmarks. Use the term where the function is unknown. Ring ditches may be the remains of ploughed out round barrows, round houses, or of modern features such as searchlight emplacements.
A manmade chamber cut into a rockface.
A set of marks found on the wall of a building, thought to be a form of sundial.
Use only if function unknown, otherwise use specific type.
A structure which protects an area of ground from the weather.
Unclassifiable site with minimal information. Specify site type wherever possible.
A building in which horses are accommodated.
A piece of stone, usually shaped, of uncertain origin or use.
Structures erected on or near a public highway.
A wooden, stone or iron post for securing things to or for preventing vehicular access to pedestrianized areas.
A post, usually of iron or concrete, used to support a street lamp.
A construction of unknown function, either extant or implied by archaeological evidence. If known, use more specific type.
An artificially raised level of ground.

A tall building, either round, square or polygonal in plan, used for a variety of purposes, including defence, as a landmark, for the hanging of bells, industrial functions, etc. Use more specific type where known.
An underground channel with a vaulted roof. Use specific type where known.
A constructed space beneath the surface of the ground.
An area of common grassland in a village used for grazing cattle, recreational purposes, etc.
An enclosing structure composed of bricks, stones or similar materials, laid in courses. Use specific type where known.
A building or room in which wood is stored.
A paved area, generally found at the back of a house.
An uncovered area, surrounded or partially surrounded by buildings.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.
A building equipped with facilities for bathing, and occasionally public baths.
A pit for the reception of night-soil and refuse.
A covered tank in which rainwater is stored for use when required.
A pipe or channel for conveying water or other liquids.
A head of water raised in a conduit system.
A small building built over the end of a water conduit or spring.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
An artificial channel for draining water or carrying it off.
A long, narrow ditch designed to carry water away from a waterlogged area.
A system of artificial or natural drains and ditches used to drain off surplus water.
Manmade constructions used to prevent water flooding the surrounding area. Often taking the form of a bank or wall but may be more elaborate e.g. the Thames Barrier.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A body of still water often artificially formed for a specific purpose. Use specifc type where known.
A toilet or toilets for public use.
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A hand operated mechanism used to raise and move water, liquids, compressed gases etc.
A wind-powered pump for land drainage.
A small pumping station.
A room or building where a pump is worked.
The receptacle at the top of a rain-water pipe which gathers the water from one or more outlets or gutters on the roof.
A large natural or artificial body of water, sometimes covered, used to collect and store water for a particular function, eg. industrial or public use.
A group of buildings in which local sewage is filtered and purified in large rectangular or circular tanks.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
A dam which can be raised or lowered to regulate the flow of water.
The gate of a sluice which can be opened or shut to let out or retain the water.
An artificial watercourse for the conveyance of water.
A pipe through which water is conducted.
A receptacle for the storage of water.
A tower serving as a reservoir to deliver water at a required point.
Buildings, engineering constructions and machinery, used for the purpose of supplying a town, etc, with water distributed through pipes.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
The structure at the top of a draw well.
A building over a well housing machinery for raising the water. Often consisting of a DONKEY WHEEL or HORSE GIN.
A multi-purpose farm building.

A multipurpose hut constructed from stone and turf, covering a square or polygonal plan. It has drystone walls and a slightly corbelled roof, usually topped with slabs. Can be either free-standing or embedded in a Cornish hedge. Particular to Cornwall.
A residence of two or three monks dependent on a foreign mother house sent to exploit a distant estate. Alien houses were officially suppressed in 1414.
A priory dependent on a foreign mother house. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
A site where alum (hydrous sulphate or salt and alumina) is quarried.
The official residence of an archbishop, eg. Lambeth Palace.
Use ABBEY with AUGUSTINIAN MONASTERY.
Use PRIORY with AUGUSTINIAN MONASTERY.

A historic term for a psychiatric hospital or institution. Refers to the infamous 13th century institution in London, called the hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem or Bethlem Royal Hospital, known for its brutal treatment of its patients.
A historic term for an institution caring for people with mental illness.
A historic term for an institution caring for people with mental illness.
Use ABBEY with AUGUSTINIAN DOUBLE HOUSE/MONASTERY/NUNNERY.
Use ALIEN PRIORY with AUGUSTINIAN DOUBLE HOUSE/MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
Use all terms.
Use PRIORY with AUGUSTINIAN MONASTERY or AUGUSTINIAN NUNNERY.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land associated with sport, leisure & entertainment. Includes sports grounds, hunting forests, cinemas, theatres etc.
Use both terms.
A building where people could bathe in salt water. Salt water was believed to have medicinal properties.
Use ABBEY and BENEDICTINE MONASTERY/NUNNERY.
Use ALIEN PRIORY with BENEDICTINE MONASTERY/NUNNERY.
Use all terms.
Use PRIORY and BENEDICTINE MONASTERY or BENEDICTINE NUNNERY.
A large, bottle-shaped,  oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
A fence that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A structure extending into the sea for the purpose of preventing further movement of washed up sand and shingle.
A site where clay is both extracted and fired to produce bricks.
Small scale enterprise producing bricks but not at the same site as the extraction of clay.
Use both terms.
Use specific type of cemetry where known.
A circle of spaced upright boulders emerging from a low, hemispherical, stony mound. The boulders may lean outwards due to pressure from the cairn material.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Use DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY, NUNNERY   or RELIGIOUS HOUSE.
An area of flattened or compacted ground used for charcoal burning.

A pit used for the re-burial of disarticulated human remains from many individuals, occasionally displaying sorting of remains, eg. grouping of skulls or long bones. Distinct from mass burials which contain articulated skeletal remains.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.
A rampart or other defensive entrenchment.
Use ABBEY and CISTERCIAN MONASTERY/NUNNERY.
Use PRIORY and CISTERCIAN MONASTERY/NUNNERY.
A factory containing machinery for processing clay for the manufacture of bricks, tiles or pottery.
Use ABBEY and CLUNIAC MONASTERY or CLUNIAC NUNNERY.
Use PRIORY and CLUNIAC MONASTERY/NUNNERY.
A place where coal is mined.
A small hut erected over a mine shaft.
Use NUNNERY, DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or RELIGIOUS HOUSE. Use with order if known.
Use HEARTH or OVEN as appropriate.
A managed small wood or thicket of underwood grown to be periodically cut to encourage new growth providing smaller timber.
Use a more specific site type where known, eg. ENCLOSURE.
A churchyard or memorial cross set on a long shaft.
A cross erected by the side of the road.
Not DENE HOLE.
Use DYKE (DEFENCE), FLOOD DEFENCES or WATER CHANNEL as appropriate.
Use both terms.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
Places of residence.
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
A small settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling with ancillary buildings.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a farm. Use more specific type where known.
Use both terms.
Military earthwork of unspecified type. Use specific site type where known.
A signpost, usually placed at a juntion or crossroads, bearing a number of individual signs radiating outward from the post to indicate locations in several directions.
A small park or enclosure where animals are kept.
Manmade constructions used to prevent rivers breaking their banks and flooding the surrounding area with water. Often taking the form of a bank or wall.
Use both terms.
The rear part of a Roman fort, where  barrack accommodation, stables and stores were situated. Use with wider site type where known.
Use Roman in a period field.
Use Roman in a period field.
Where building foundation use specific site type where known.
