A meeting hall of the Temperance Society.
A building where military officers are accommodated.

A place of worship for members of the Congregational Church. These churches, the first of which was founded in 1616 in Southwark, practised self government. Most of them were merged to form the United Reformed Church in 1972.
A training college for the instruction of military trainees in the theory and practice of warfare.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
Use both terms.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
A place of worship for followers of the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion, a Calvinistic Methodist sect founded in the 1740s by Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon.
A place of meeting and worship for Brethren, a fundamentalist puritan sect founded in Ireland in the late 1820s and established in England in Plymouth in the 1830s.
A place of worship for Christian Scientists, a sect founded in the mid-19th century in America who believe that God is the only reality and can bring healing to humanity.
A place where the homeless are accommodated, permanently or temporarily.
A building used by the church to promote Christianity through lectures, study, etc.
A non residential building providing recreational, social and other facilities, especially for the elderly and those with special needs.
A place of worship for Calvinistic Methodists, Welsh Methodists who split from the established church in 1811.
A place of worship for members of the Church of Scotland which has been Presbyterian since 1690. It is the national Church of Scotland and is free and endowed.

A place of worship for Strict Baptists, a sect who broke away from the Particular Baptists and kept up the practice of denying communion to non members after the union of General and Particular Baptists was formed in 1891.
A plant for bottling manufactured goods, as opposed to a BOTTLE WORKS where bottles were made.

A place of worship for Presbyterians, a movement who started off attempting to reform Anglicanism before breaking away in 1660. Sometimes referred to as moderate puritans, they joined with the Congregationalists to form the United Reformed church in 1972.
A place of worship for Unitarians, a movement which does not believe in the Trinity but only in the Unity of Christ. Christ was to them just an exalted human teacher.
A place of worship for followers of the Pentecost (ie. emphasising the gifts of the Holy Spirit).
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
A floating structure consisting of two walls standing on pontoon tanks, the latter of which can be flooded to receive a vessel and then pumped out until the pontoon deck and the ship are dry.
The hull of a dismantled ship used as a prison.
A floating structure designed to resist the force of waves.
A floating bridge, generally temporary, whose decks are supported on low flat-bottomed or hollow floats.
A form of floating, moveable pier designed for use in open water.
A small building housing a mechanism used for winding a cable.
A building or site from which a lookout can be kept.
A room containing copper or steel vessels in which hops are added to the basic beer mixture.
A building used to house calves.
A centre for the teaching of crafts.

A place of worship for Wesleyan Methodists. This was the original Methodist church from which the other denominations seceded. In 1932 they joined the United Methodists and the Primitive Methodists to form the Methodist church.
A small roofed shelter for cattle without tethering point or stalls, but with a small yard attached. It is often detached from the main range of farm buildings.
A site where household rubbish and other waste products can be disposed of. May take the form of a pit, rubbish tip, landfill site or incineration plant.
Prehistoric structure consisting of three or more standing stones in close proximity to each other, forming an unroofed approximately rectangular structure open in one direction.
Areas of indeterminate function.
a wooden, metal or stone post used to tether a horse, or other animals.
A site where metal is worked. Use specific type where known.
Living quarters for animals, birds, etc, as pets or for observation, entertainment, etc.
A building where reptiles are accommodated at a zoo or wildlife park.
A zoo building containing artificial ponds or tanks in which aquatic plants and animals are kept alive for purposes of observation and study.
A temporary kitchen set up in the field providing food for troops. Use with MILITARY CAMP if existence of this is known.
A group of planted trees or shrubs, generally of uniform age and of a single species.
Circular enclosure featuring an enclosing bank with no accompanying ditch. Use specific type where known.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A site where clay is mined from the ground.
A site where barytes (barium sulphate) is mined. Barytes is also commonly worked from the waste tips of lead mines.
A mine used for the extraction of the mineral Witherite. When secondary mineral, use with term for product, eg. LEAD MINE.
When a secondary mineral, use term for product type, eg. LEAD MINE.
A site where fluorspar or fluoride of calcium, often used as a flux by copper-ore smelters, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A single ditched 3-sided rectilinear enclosure.
A site where gypsum and anhydrate is mined.

Ditches interrupted by wide, regular causeways. Each section of ditch is about 30-40m long, and each causeway is 10-15m wide. In some cases, a network of fields has been created. Found mainly in the South East of England.
A place where osiers (willows) are grown for basket-making.
Use broader site type where known
A place where umber or oxide of iron and manganese, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of football is played.
A pedestrianized shopping street, or a more complex arrangement of shopping 'squares' and walkways.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
An area in a town where traffic is prohibited, often containing shops.
A bridge carrying a tramway.
A house, the inhabitant of which keeps an official register e.g. a registrar's house near a cemetery would keep an official record of deaths and burials.
Long alignment of cairns lying between two large cairns; first recognized as a site type on Sourton Tor, Dartmoor.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
A place where boats are stored.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A building where masts are made and stored.
Workshop for the painting of vehicles, machines, etc.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
A cairn featuring a mound of small diameter (normally less than 6m), which is surrounded by a kerb of stones which are considerably taller than the mound.
A structure used for the storage of coal.
A site where granite is excavated.
Production of smokeless domestic fuel by roasting anthracite in a type of kiln.
A rescue station serving a number of mines in the immediate area.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A building or range of buildings used for the cleaning, crushing and loading of freshly mined coal.
A structure housing machinery for crushing coal. Usually found at the pithead of a colliery or coal mine.
An unidentified feature on the seabed recorded by fishermen as an obstruction to trawling.
Water spraying tower for cooling coke after it emerges from the furnace.
A building forming part of a colliery ventilation system exhausting stale air from shafts and headings.
A flat, and usually level area of mown and cultivated grass, attached to a house.
A pile of rough stones and soil used for the growing of ferns and other plants.
A garden which consists of rocks and rock-loving plants that require little water.
A place devoted to the cultivation and exhibition of rare trees.
A garden in which a variety of plants are grown to encourage butterflies.
A garden incorporating fountains and pools in which aquatic and other water-loving plants are grown.
A box or place of confinement for animals, made wholly or partly of wire, wood or bars of metal, so as to admit air and light.
A 20th century feature found in public parks and seaside resorts. The face of the clock is planted with low-growing flowers and plants, while the moving hands are covered with small foliage.
A building where advice, counselling and medical treatment is available.
Buildings and works around a mine shaft with an artificial embankment on which the winding gear etc, is located.
A straight mine entrance, driven on a constant downwards slope.

A building housing the permanent electricity generator supply for domestic use or small scale unspecified power generation on an airfield. Unlike stand by set houses, power houses had to cope with both essential and non-essential loads.
A site where methane gas, released by coal mining, is collected and processed.
A garden in which flower beds are the primary focal point.
A long bed planted with perennial flowers and plants.
A garden, often geometrical in layout, or area for the cultivation of roses.
A piece of land, sometimes man-made, completely surrounded by water.
A decorative garden, often landscaped, laid out with intricate flower beds and hedges, and often containing ornate sculptures, fountains and garden ornaments.
A fall of water. Use for artificial waterfalls if naturalistic in form, otherwise use CASCADE.
Obstacles such as scaffolding, barbed wire and concrete blocks or cylinders placed on a beach to impede the progress of enemy soldiers, vehicles or watercraft landing from the sea.
A framework, often made of steel,  supporting a crane or similar structure, or for supporting a platform or stage.
A cluster of piles for mooring a vessel.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
A room or building housing the controls to a mechanized system, eg. in a power station, airport, etc.
A building, structure or site used for the storage of charcoal.
A building in a military complex (eg. naval dockyard, castle, etc.) for preparing gunpowder.
A building in which the ingredients of an explosive charge are weighed into their correct proportions and mixed prior to incorporation.
A building containing equipment used for the polishing of grains of gunpowder and extraction of the resulting dust.
Accommodation in hired rooms or a lodging house.
For broadcast radio programmes use BROADCASTING TRANSMITTER, for radar transmissions use TRANSMITTER SITE.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Order of Tiron.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Premonstratensian order.
Open yard for keeping cattle in during winter. Used from the mid-14th century in drier, Eastern, arable counties.
A building or group of buildings containing equipment capable of transmitting and receiving radio signals. Use BROADCASTING RADIO STATION for broadcasting establishments e.g. BBC Radio stations.
Graves known to be of shipwreck victims buried close to their site of discovery, as was customary until the 19th century, rather than in consecrated ground.
A holding on a smaller-scale than an ordinary farm.
A small stone structure, usually at a spring or bog, in which dairy products were kept cool on slate shelves.
A site, including hangars, moorings and ancillary buildings, used for the storage, maintenance, take off and landing of airships.
A small brick structure attached to a house for keeping fish prior to cooking.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
Grinding mill for producing dyes and pigments from natural materials.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice shooting by aerial, seaborne or land mounted weapons.
A site where a single large balloon was attached by fine wire cables to the ground to form an aerial obstruction to attacking enemy aircraft.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templars
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Gilbertine order.
A 19th century glasshouse built specifically for the fostering of camellias.
An 18th century garden building, designed in the style of a classical Ionic temple, used for standing or sitting in.
An 18th century garden building, designed in the form of a classical Doric temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A building used for the shelter and protection of deer, especially in winter.
A level space in a garden occupied by ornamental flower beds.
An often secluded garden set below the level of surrounding ground, usually surrounded with terraces.
A peat-based garden where various types of heather are grown.
A garden created within woodland where imported species such as camellias, magnolias and rhododendrons are grown.
A garden with one or more platforms with walks, often on different levels, usually close to the house.
Use both terms.

Originally an area planted with evergreens or winter-flowering plants for winter display, they can also be large glasshouses built for public entertainment where the original purpose of displaying plants has either disappeared or been minimalised.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
A lattice work bower or shady retreat covered with climbing plants.
A closely mown lawn used for the game of croquet.
A garden for the cultivation of herbs used for medicinal or culinary purposes.
A garden where woodland and meadow flowers grow in an apparently natural way.
An intricately designed garden in which ground coves, low shrubs or coloured earths are arranged in interlacing patterns resembling knots
A garden containing trees or shrubs pruned and trained into various geometric, zoomorphic or fantastic shapes.
A walk bordered by trees or clipped hedges in a garden or park. Made of gravel, sand or turf, it is different from a path or avenue.
A place where goods are sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
Floor cover in Roman time, where small cubes (tesserea) of one or more colours were laid in a geometric pattern.
A multi-storey building in which individual blocks of flats cluster around a central service core.
A small house or a portion of a house used as a self-contained apartment.
A place where a product is given any finishing processes before being despatched to the user.
A type of warehouse, usually one-storeyed.
A place where vehicles can be filled up with petrol, oil, water, etc.
A water-filled structure for experimental research.
The area surrounding a monastic house including conventual buildings, outbuildings, cemetery, fishponds, etc, usually marked out by a bank and/or ditch or precinct wall.
A large bed surrounded by an earthwork and filled with composing vegetable matter and animal waste. This was used to produce Nitre, a constituent of gunpowder.
A land based establishment armed with torpedoes and used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A group of buildings and machines, usually situated close to the pithead,  enabling the rapid, mechanized loading of goods wagons with coal.

A spatially discrete scatter of mixed artefactual material found on the ground, seabed or riverbed which may have been deposited over time rather than resulting from one particular event. Index particular types where appropriate.
Originally a large tract of wooded country, owned by the Monarchy, for the purpose of hunting. The royal parks of London, eg. Greenwich, are all open to the public and have been for centuries.
A hopper for the storage of ash.
A mill used for the manufacture of narrow strips of woven fabric used in the closing or fixing of garments, or for binding the edges of fabric goods.

A large communal room often occupying the full height of the building, used for functions such as meetings, entertainments etc. Traditionally found in medieval buildings but also found in later buildings emulating medieval architecture.
A factory used for the manufacture of screws.
A pit or emplacement surrounding a concrete pedestal, or 'thimble', which was used to mount a spigot mortar. Deployed by the Home Guard during WWII as an anti invasion measure.
A burial site for animals.
A building or site for watching specific military activities or the movement of enemy forces, etc.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where cargo vessels can load and unload large storage containers. May include a rail terminal for containers which have been transported to the port by rail.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using ferry services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A large building used for the storage of grain.
A tall, metal structure erected as a support for electric power cables.
A shore establishment for the teaching of maritime theory and practical skills.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply for domestic use.
A building associated with a spinning mill in which raw material is mechanically spun into yarn or thread.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
A textile building where the process of combing, a preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
Recovery and removal of grease (lanolin) from raw wool.
A large store where wool is stored.
Posts with hooks attached to allow drying new cloth to be stretched out between them.
A building in which wool or cotton were beaten to clean and separate the fibres.
Shed for grinding rags, eg. for use in mungo and shoddy mills.
A building or structure in which processed cloth is dried.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
A factory where food is preserved either by freezing, salting or pickling
A complex of purpose-built or adapted buildings used for the maintenance, storage, assembly and control of sea mines and minefields.
A warehouse, usually under the charge of CUSTOM HOUSE officials, in which goods were stored before the duty had been paid. Often found in dockyards, harbours, etc.
A market where fish is sold.
An often stately or ornate entrance to a railway tunnel.
Use both terms.
Dry dock for the repair of ships.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A storehouse using mechanical means of controlling temperature rather than ice or insulation.
A place for recreation with electronic game machines and gambling machines.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
For the disposal of town refuse. Some 19th century plants were linked to a power station. Later ones incorporate INCINERATORS, recycling facilities, etc.
A railway station or platform built specifically for the loading and unloading of goods.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A building or room, where business and/or administrative activities to do with the canals was conducted.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
A building or set of rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls were held.
Use both terms.
A place where ropes are made.
The entrance to a tunnel. Use more specific type where known.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
An underground bomb-proof structure used as a command centre for military operations.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A pier where passsengers can embark and disembark and goods can be transferred to and from vessels.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
A high building at an airport from which air traffic is controlled by radio.
Use both terms.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
Use both terms.
A long ridge of earth, rocks or gravel primarily constructed to carry a roadway.
An engine used for directly winding up coal from deep mines, first used in the 18th century.
An underground passageway for cables, pipes and pedestrians to allow passage beneath an over ground obstacle.
Building housing switch gear to control electricity supply either to the National Grid, industrial or domestic premises.
Use both terms.

A series of parallel railway sidings on which goods wagons originating from different locations can be sorted or re-sorted into new trains before being despatched to their next destination or sorting points.
A large building or structure where coal is washed, sized and graded before being sold.
A large structure, found at sports stadiums, from where television or radio broadcasts are made of the sporting events.
A large board found at sporting events, erected so as to be seen by the spectators, on which the score of a game is kept.
A crane, located in an engineering workshop or similar establishment, which can be moved on rails and thus used anywhere within the workshop.
A council-owned block of flats.
A building adjoining a cricket pitch with facilities for players and spectators.
A place where hats are made and sold.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
A building where miners could improve their knowledge by attending lectures and using the reading room facilities.
A stable, on two or more levels.
A building providing accommodation, dining facilities and recreation for non commissioned officers.
A large body of water surrounded by land.
An area where the sport of wrestling takes place.
A depot used for the unloading of coal.
A freestanding staff upon which a flag is hung.

A structure for transferring coal from railway coal waggons onto a ship for onward transport to market, normally at least in part using gravity, and also occasionally from railway coal waggons to road vehicles.

A building within a complex, such as a leisure centre, school, industrial site etc, often containing toilet and washing facilities, where individuals can change their clothes. For a changing room within a larger building, see Components.
A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.
A building used in the preparation of manure.
An ancilliary building, usually to provide gas for lighting a particular building (eg. railway stations, factories, etc) as opposed to public GAS WORKS.
A barn with steam powered threshing.
A factory where pencils are manufactured.
Series of wire mesh screens used for grading lumps of coal according to size.
A place where pheasants are reared and kept.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
An iron, stone or concrete tower built up from the bed of a reservoir. From it the control valves of the pipes which draw off water at different levels are operated.
A tank or pond containing a layer of sand etc, for filtering large quantities of liquid.
A watertight reservoir or tank that receives sewage, and by sedimentation and bacterial action effects a process of partial purification.
A purpose built quay for supplying ships with fuel.
An office used by a qualified pilot, expert in ship-handling and with local knowledge, who assists the captain or master to take a vessel in or out of a harbour or through narrow waters.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
Earthworks and buildings added around a bastion to enhance protection of the bastion.
A factory or plant used for the manufacture of electrical machinery or components.
A shed in which delicate plants are reared from seedlings for planting out later.
Use for stationary railway carriage being used for a purpose it wasn't originally intended for - office, shelter, etc.
A college where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
Structures associated with telecommunications.
A floating, fixed marker used to indicate to a navigator a sea area to approach or avoid.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a village of small houses accommodating a small group.""
A residential establishment for the care and accommodation of children and young people.
A structure consisting of a large, metal framework holding a skyward facing dish. Used for transmitting and receiving signals which are relayed by satellite.
An artificial hill constructed in Tudor gardens, especially, to provide a good view.
A raised platform for the unloading of coal from waggons or other containers.
A room or building occupied by a person employed to keep accounts of workers' hours of labour.
An administrative building used by the official in charge of a dock or harbour.
A purpose-built terrace of shops.
A building with facilities for playing snooker.
A store belonging to a cooperative society.
A road or way for riding on horseback within a park or estate.
Flats or houses first built by 19th century philanthropic societies as a model to encourage the development of approved working class housing.
A room or suite of rooms used as dwellings, eg. in private houses, hotels or tenement houses.
Engineering works dedicated solely to the manufacture and repair of boilers.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently low to be seen below low lying cloud. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a Low Light is usually accompanied by a HIGH LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
Steam engine, usually, driving a centrifugal fan to provide an air blast for a blast furnace.

A roughly circular monument featuring a low, more or less level platform of stones surrounded or retained by a low stone kerb. Some may feature a small central open area, thus resembling a ring cairn.
A building or buildings where explosives are manufactured.

Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of pottery. Use only for sites where there is evidence of pottery manufacture but no specific monument, otherwise use more specific term.
A group of buildings and satellite dishes used to transmit and receive signals relayed by satellites.

A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
A building used for the collection and storage of electricity using large lead-acid batteries (accumulators).
A coke-filled tower used for the dissolving and neutralising of acid produced by alkali-making processes.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.

A separate hospital building, or block of an asylum, where new arrivals were segregated from old inmates for a defined period. This system was developed from the mid-19th century onwards.
Religious establishment, founded in Somerset, where free love was practised.
A historic term for an institution caring for older, destitute women.
Buildings, structures or sites used for the production of chemicals used in agriculture, such as fertilizers and weed killers.
Small engineering works specialising in the production of items such as ploughs and threshing machinery.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A site for the sale or hire of agricultural machinery.
The premises of an agricultural merchant where agricultural equipment, animal feed and fertilizers can be bought.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the control, accommodation, service and testing of aircraft.
A factory where aircraft engines are assembled.
Sites used for the manufacture of aircraft.
A large metal pylon structure used to tether airships.

A historic term for an institution offering care and accommodation for alcoholic women, an alternative to the workhouse for the destitute.
A building or area within a brewery where barrels of ale are stored.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A sports pitch usually with a synthetic surface (ie. not grass).
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
A factory producing metallic aluminium by an electrolysis process.
A place where ambulances are serviced and maintained.
A concept dating in England from the second half of the 18th century, when hardy North American plants were relatively easy to obtain.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious woman or nun, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
The principal Anglican church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
A place of worship and residence for Anglican nuns.
Including accommodation for animals, birds, reptiles and fish in captivity.
A monument commemorating an animal.
Buildings and structures associated with the use of animals to generate power.
Buildings or sites used in the production of items derived from the parts of animals not used for consumption.
A stall where animals are kept individually.
A burial site for an animal, usually commemorated by a gravestone or other structure.
A place or building where animals can be washed. Often in the form of a pool with a walled funnel-like structure enabling animals to be guided into the pool.
A building, range of buildings or site, for the accommodation, rearing and/or treatment of animals, birds and fish, both wild and domestic.
An area within a hospital concerned with the care and medical treatment of expectant mothers.
A reinforced concrete block designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Use more specific type where known.

An indoor market used for the sale of antique goods.
A road, sometimes raised as a causeway, which serves as an approach road to a building or bridge.
The residence and office of an archdeacon.
An educational establishment where the art and theory of building and construction is taught.

An armoured fighting vehicle. Often survive as commemorative monuments, targets and coastal wrecks.
Buildings and structures associated with educational and artistic recreational activities.
A training establishment for gunnery personnel.
An apartment, usually with a north-light, used by artists.

A large space in an underground tunnel, usually wider than the tunnel itself, used for storage, etc.
A lime kiln in which coal is burnt, as distinct from a flame-free kiln in which wood or peat is used.
A mill which is powered by a turbine.
Seats or benches covered in turf, built against a wall, tree or fountain,  were a common feature of medieval enclosed gardens.
Garden steps covered in turf.
Mechanism for turning around vehicles in a confined space.
A barrier which rotates on an axis and is usually so arranged as to allow a person to pass through  an opening only in one direction.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
A car park situated beneath the surface of the ground.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
A section of road that provides a passage beneath another road or railway.
A waterwheel where the inflow of water strikes the paddles or floatboards well below the axis of the wheel, ie. the water more or less passes under it.
Area in a brewery used for the production of beer by the Burton Union method.

A place of worship for members of the United Reformed Church, a group formed in 1972 by the amalgamation of most of the Congregational Churches in England and Wales with the Presbyterian Church in England.
An office where the administrative duties of a university are performed.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.

Areas within the urban environment with their surfaces open to the sky, that have been consciously acquired or publicly regulated to serve urban shaping function, in addition others may provide recreational opportunities.
A model village built by a utopian society or group of artists.
A small building housing a valve which controls the flow within a water regulation system.
A building, or room within a brewery, where beer or cider undergoes fermentation in vats or tuns.
A garden devoted to the growth of vegetables.
Sites associated with the manufacture and engineering of vehicles.
A centre where patients suffering from venereal and associated diseases receive treatment.
A tall stack used to disperse foul air from the bottom of a mine.
Small furnace, used to create an upward draught of air in mine workings.
A forester's cottage.
A meeting hall of the verderers, who were the officers appointed to maintain the King's forests.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder. Extensively used as mine winding engines.
A hospital for the medical or surgical treatment of domestic or wild animals.
A rural school serving a number of villages, built in Cambridgeshire in the 1930s.
A point in a village providing water for drinking and washing.
A glass-house or hot-house constructed for the cultivation of a grapevine.
A building or complex, often associated with a historic site or place of interest, containing interpretation panels and information for visitors to the site or area.
A school built and/or supported by voluntary contributions.
A place or path for walking in a park or garden. Use more specific type where possible.
A small crane fixed to the wall of a warehouse or similar building.
A substantial monument attached to a wall and often standing on the floor.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
Non-pavilion type of attached ward block.
A building or room within a monastery in which the monks were allowed to warm themselves. The warming house was often the only place where a fire was allowed.
A ditch or channel, cut or used to carry silt-laden water from the river to the area to be warped and back to the river once the silt has settled out on to the land.
A pit or tank where the chemicals used in tanning are washed from the animal hides.
Outdoor site for domestic washing, etc.
A building containing a range of processes for cleaning and processing metallic ores.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the disposal of domestic and industrial waste.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, and later used to direct air traffic. Use more specific type where known.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
A small building used as a shelter by a constable of the watch responsible for patrolling the streets at night to safeguard life and property.
A structure consisting of a large plastic pipe attached to a high tower and sloping down to a swimming pool. Water flows down the inside allowing people to slide down into the pool below.
A garden building or greenhouse, containing pools in which Water Lilies are grown.
A water tank, often raised on stilts, used to supply water to steam trains.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of water power.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
Buildings, structures and sites for regulating the flow of water.
Sites, building, structures & features associated with the supply & drainage of water & the disposal of sewage and waste water. Includes bodies of water, waterways & associated ancillary structures.
A water point with a device to regulate the flow of water.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with water transport.
A large, undergound watercourse.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
A house occupied by an employee of a waterworks. Usually found in association with a pumping station or waterworks.
A water pump situated at the side of a road or track for use by travellers and their animals.
A continuous row of WEALDEN HOUSES.
An apparatus for weighing people, animals or things.
A chapel adjacent to, associated with or containing a well.
A lid for a well. Well covers are often ornate and can be made of various materials.
The residence of a well keeper.
Use both terms.
A circle made out of stones, which is used for making wheels.
A garden deliberately planted with white plants and shrubs.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
A market where goods are bought and sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A large storehouse where wholesale goods are stored.
A place where wigs, hair-pieces and hair extensions are made and sold.
A stationary hoisting machine consisting of a rotating drum around which a cable, rope or chain is attached.
A building housing a winching mechanism.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of wind power.
An area of ground indicating the site of a horse or man-powered winding mechanism.
Use both terms.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of wine and cider.
A licenced establishment where wine and other alcoholic drinks are sold for drinking on the premises.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A press in which the juice is extracted from grapes in the manufacture of wine.
An establishment where wine is produced.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of women and children.
A specialist hospital where women receive medical and surgical treatment.
A building used by members of the Womens Institute, an organization which meets regularly and engages in various social and cultural activities.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
Includes processing and manufacturing of all forms of wood.
Manufacture and use of wood side products, ie. unprocessed wood rather than processed timber.
A road surface made out of wooden blocks or planks. It was much used in English cities before 1940, but the cost of wooden blocks eventually made it uneconomical.
A site where unprocessed wood is used to manufacture goods.
A barn used for the storage and drying of wool.
A building used to dry wool in.
A room or building used for the storage of fleeces.
Includes worsted and other wool-related textiles.
A structure used for drying yarn in open fields.
A workshop in which carded wool was passed through heated combs to straighten and separate the long and short fibres prior to spinning. Associated with the worsted branch of the textile industry.
Use both terms.

Use both terms.
A college founded for the education and betterment of the working classes. Lectures usually being held after the end of the working day.
A place where working men could educate themselves through lectures and the use of a reading room with newspapers, etc.
A heated room or building used to dry yarn after it has been washed.
A building associated with rope manufacture, especially in naval dockyards.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
A garden where yew and other coniferous trees are grown.
A garden walk lined with yew trees and hedges.
A path across a road marked with black and white stripes where pedestrians may cross.
An area for the testing of rockets and guided missiles. Includes all structures associated with both the firing and testing of rockets and missiles.
A metal structure supporting high powered lights.
A site available to the public for the pursuit of leisure and recreational activities.
The subsoil traces of prehistoric cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of an ard to till the soil.
A specially prepared track used for fast motorcycle racing.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
Use for miniaturized monument type. Index with actual monument type where possible.
A site where small electrical goods such as radios, lamps and heaters are manufactured.
A shelter for the storage of bicycles.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
A structure used for music, dance, ceremonial or civic events.
An office for the issuing of government stamps and receiving of stamp duty.
An educational establishment where law is taught.
The residence of a person employed in the textile industry.
A garden or collection of potted plants on the flat roof of a house or other building.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
A building in which the lay sisters resided. Lay sisters were not nuns and as such weren't bound by any vows. They could leave the convent and even marry if they wished.
An explosive-proof vaulted chamber used for the storage or ordnance.
A large store for the temporary accommodation of goods awaiting transportation to or from the sea.
A building where sugar is stored.
A slate situated at the end of a terrace for a coal company employee to wake the miners for their shift. The slate had the time of the shifts written on it.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
A house in a terrace built on top of another, with access at high and low level to either side.
The residence of a lifeboatman.
A building associated with the legal administration of a forest, eg. Forest of Dean.
A post, made of wood, metal or other material, erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons such as measurement, calibration etc.
A chapel for the use of travellers and pilgrims.
A public recreational complex centred around an open-air swimming pool. Use SWIMMING POOL as a component of LIDO.
The residence of a glover.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.
A house of Roman Catholic nuns or canonesses.
A usually south-facing wall used for the cultivation of fruit plants.
A friary of the Order of the Friar servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites. The Servite Fathers came to England in 1864.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
A site used by a carrier to accommodate his horses and vehicles and store goods awaiting transportation, etc.
Place where food or money was handed out to the poor.
A building for the storage of unbleached, untreated fabric.
A low, hemispherical cairn surrounded by a freestanding, continuous circle of boulders.
Use appropriate term.

A long, narrow, irregularly constructed and generally unstructured mound of stones. Normally a by-product of field clearance for agricultural purposes, though prehistoric examples may include burials and other deposits.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of spaced post- holes which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A pit alignment accompanied by a linear bank (or banks) running parallel and adjacent to the line(s) of pits.
A round barrow containing or covering a number of burials. Use both terms.

A subsidiary enclosure externally attached to an enclosure of known or unknown date and function. The annexe is generally smaller than, and secondary to, the main enclosure. Use more specific site type where known. Do not use for Roman military sites.
A large building, situated by or near a dock, canal, road or railway and used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.
A temporary airfield in use during the build-up to D-Day. They consisted of a natural earth or grass surface reinforced with wire mesh.
Gun battery built specifically to mount short range weapons to defend a beach against an attempted landing.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
Used where an existing building is designated as the residence of an official.
A building in which textile rags are sorted according to fibre types.
Use for distinct structure on a large scale.
A building used to house apes and monkeys.
A house used to accommodate camels, often found at a zoo or wildlife park.
A building used to accommodate hippopotami.
Complex of buildings and structures associated with the testing of jet engines.

A hole in the ground which has been created by driving or hammering an upright stake into the ground. As a feature of some archaeological sites they may often represent the only surviving evidence for the former presence of an above-ground structure.
A nunnery of nuns belonging to the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites.
A place where injured or endangered animals are kept and looked after.

Nowadays a hospital block where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical and surgical treatment. Formerly a place where psychiatric patients were primarily segregated from other patients in a hospital.
A disused term for a hospital block where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders are treated and cared for. Previously a segregated area separate from other hospital patient wards.
A building housing a number of power looms.
A place of worship for followers of the teachings of Martin Luther.
A house having four rooms of equal height on each of two floors; in larger houses there are often two parallel and equal roofs.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.
A basement or cellar, usually within a house, leased as a separate dwelling.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
An area of ground or water containing explosive mines.
WWII secret bases, sometimes partially underground, intended for use by the British resistance in the eventuality of a foreign invasion.
An RAF Base, used specifically for the storage and maintenance of barrage balloons.
A building containing a machine tool for boring out large cylindrical holes in items such as steam engine cylinders, pump barrels, etc.
A public music or dancing establishment often with facilities for gambling.
A stall, often within a cow house, where cattle are kept individually.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A site showing some signs of occupation but evidence is insufficient to imply permanent settlement.
A wall containing apertures to allow a weapon to be fired through it.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
A factory, or group of buildings, containing apparatus used to extract specific properties, e.g flavour or scent, from natural ingredients.
A school where Jewish children are educated.

A structure or building used in the manufacture of the explosive cordite. After the cordite had been pressed to extract moisture it was placed on racks within the stove prior to being taken to the reeling house for winding.
A building where mineral jelly was stored. Mineral jelly was used as a stabilizer in the manufacture of the explosive, cordite.
A building used for the storage of explosives of a non-military function, eg. mining explosives, signal explosivres etc.
The residence of a master shipwright.
A structure, often ornamental, in a garden, park or area of recreation, designed to reflect the style of Indian architecture. The most famous example of which is the Royal Pavilion in Brighton.
A round or polygonal building containing a wheel turned by an ox to provide power.
A lodging for itinerant Irish labourers.
A large board, often attached to the side of a building, on which advertisements can be displayed. Use for external structures only.
The rigging mast of a sailing ship erected as a monument. Used for naval displays.
A covered stall at a market or fair, etc.
A three-sided structure for the production and storage of silage.
An embanked shute, often stone paved, allowing carts to tip their loads of coal from the road into a storage area.
A curved structural span which is supported at the sides or ends. May vary in shape from the horizontal flat arch through semicircular and semielliptical forms.
A type of bridge which has machinery and movable elements, eg. to allow vessels to pass.
A bridge whose deck is directly supported from pylons by straight cables without vertical suspenders.
A specialized form of truss bridge that extends or cantilevers from both sides of the pier, the inner 'arms' usually supporting a central span.
A bridge supported by large beams or girders, originally of wood or iron, now usually of steel or reinforced concrete.
A bridge made up of many relatively small members joined together in a series of interconnecting triangles.

A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of lithic artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context. Use particular types where appropriate.

A site which has produced evidence of in situ working of stone for the manufacture of tools, weapons or other objects. Such sites will usually, but not always, be of prehistoric date. Use object material where known.
The approximate location at which stray finds of artefacts were found. Index with object name.
A furnace used for melting metals for casting or for heating shot.
Use for flood defence embankment.
Sites, buildings and structures for the control and mounting of anti aircraft artillery. Also, structures for passive or indirect defence against enemy aircraft.
Sites and buildings used in the coordination of the defence of the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.
Sites, buildings and structures for the defence of the coastline from sea and air invasion.
Sites and structures, often un-manned, intended to impede or confuse enemy forces.
Buildings, structures and sites directly associated with the operation of military airfields. See also AIR TRANSPORT SITE in the TRANSPORT Class.
Buildings, structures and sites for the detection of encroaching enemy forces.
Buildings and structures used for sending and receiving signals.
An ancilliary building or structure associated with a military base. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
Buildings, structures and sites for the training of military personnel.
Sites and structures for the transport of military personnel, vehicles and armaments.
Distinctive clerestory-roofed building, used for the drying and storage of military parachutes.
A combination of obstructions, used either to stop enemy forces or force them off the road.
Usually a small, two or three man trench, dug as an isolated fieldwork rather than as part of a defensive system. A WWI and WWII feature.
A purpose-built or adapted structure intended as a headquarters for an air raid precautions warden.
A complex of buildings and earthworks constructed for the storage of bombs and pyrotechnics.
A nonconformist church for the followers of Edward Irving.
A building with first aid facilities to deal with accidents and other medical emergencies.
A building used for the treatment of victims of chemical, gas or other forms of contamination.
A wall, usually of reinforced concrete, designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle
Use both terms.

An upright, or originally upright, stone featuring a hole which is often large enough in diameter for a person to pass through, eg. Men an Tol, Cornwall. Do not use for perforated portable stone artefacts.
A building or structure used for the storage of sugar.
A place of residence and worship for Anglican monks.
A mechanism used to turn a trolleybus around.
A place of worship for followers of Sikhism.
A large building where iron is stored.
A raised platform or walkway connecting two buildings or a ship with the quay, etc.
A building used by an organization instituted to promote the needs and rights of the blind.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
Use both terms.
The residence of a herder.
A place of worship for followers of Hinduism.
A specialist school for the teaching of deaf people.
Use both terms.
A concrete structure designed to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was only intended to be occupied during an attack.
Use both terms.
Use both terms.
A building, on a military airfield or base, in which motor vehicles are housed.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.
Floatable vessel used as a floodgate in docks.

A hospital ward block, completely open on the south side apart from a low railing and sun blind. It was thought beneficial for the recovery of wounded soldiers as well as those with diseases of the chest.
Small revolving wooden chalets that could be turned with their backs to the prevailing wind so that hospital patients could recline in them on long chairs in all weathers.
A building of unknown purpose found at a military site. Use more specific type where known.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used as accommodation for the armed forces and, during WWII, as emergency housing for bombed out civilians. Also used for storage.
Use both terms.
An area of cultivated, managed woodland producing wood which is used for a variety of purposes.
A Roman cremation burial in which the human cremated remains are placed inside or adjacent to a wooden casket, frequently decorated with lion-headed mounts and studs.
A place where patients have X-Rays taken to highlight an illness or irregularity.
Rolls of barbed wire with supporting metal posts designed to impede enemy advance.
A protective structure, often made of sandbags with reinforcement, designed to protect aircraft at airfields from enemy attack.
A building used to coordinate civil defence in times of war. Can also be utilized as aid centres in times of national emergency.
A WWII structure designed to project sheets of flame across an area such as a beach, the sea or a road, to hinder attacking forces.
A place from where rescue missions are co-ordinated and casualties treated after an accident, offensive action or disaster.
An undefined structure used in the training of people in a certain skill.
A military building from which the guns of a battery were directed.
An instrument used for making a loud sound for information or warning.
A building or group of buildings, often enclosed by a system of fortifications, used by an armed force for the storage and distribution of military equipment.
A building housing a generator.

A complex of buildings at a seaport, comprising of a terminal building, landing pier and hangars, used for the embarkation of passengwers and/or freight on flying boat services during the 1930's-50's.
A site where the magnetic signature of ships was lowered thereby making them less susceptible to magnetic mines.
An abandoned settlement, usually of the Medieval period, often visible only as earthworks or on aerial photographs.
An ancillary building to a synagogue, used as a place of worship at the feast of the tabernacle.
A hospital where Royal Naval personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
An establishment where books, periodicals, music, etc, are produced from original manuscripts and distributed to booksellers, dealers and the public.
A hospital department concerned with the reconstruction or repair of parts of the human body using transferred tissue, either in the treatment of injury or for cosmetic reasons.
Use both terms.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
A hospital department for the identification and treatment of skin tissue disorders.

A large hilltop or hillslope enclosure in South West England, located close to rock outcrops, and surrounded by one or more circuits of stone built walls. All are prehistoric; some are definitely Neolithic.
A place of worship and residence for followers of Buddha.
A building, site or structure associated with the demonstration and testing of weapons and military equipment.
A purpose-built trench used to test chemical warfare weapons.
A place of worship for Welsh Presbyterians. Formerly known as Calvinistic Methodists, the Presbyterian Church of Wales separated from the established church in 1811.
A place of meeting and worship for Exclusive Brethren, an exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
A place of meeting and worship for Open Brethren, a non exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group founded in Manchester who broke away from the Methodists in 1806.
A place of worship for Protestant Methodists, a group who broke away from the Methodists to form their church in Leeds in 1828.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Association. This group split from the Methodists in 1836 and were separate until joining the Methodist Reform Church in 1857.

SCOPE_NOTE: A place of worship for members of the New Connexion of General Baptists,an orthodox Baptist church which broke away from the General Baptists in 1770 when the latter became influenced by Unitarianism.
A place of worship for members of the Romanian Orthodox Church, the national church of Romania.
A building, factory or works which was engaged in the manufacture of refining saltpetre. Often part of a gunpowder works.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of ammonal explosives.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of the explosive bellite.
A works or factory principally engaged in the manufacture of dynamite
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the explosive Gelignite.
A factory or works engaged in the manufacture of the explosive guncotton. They may be found as separate factories or form part of a cordite factory.
A factory or works principally engaged in the production of a single base propellant, using nitrocellulose without the addition of nitroglycerine.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the mining explosive sabulite.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
A works using sealed retorts to produce charcoal. Wood distillates may be produced as byproducts of this process. They may be found at separate works or comprise part of a gunpowder works.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of gunpowder.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of explosives.
A factory principally engaged in the  manufacture of the propellant explosive cordite.
A factory or works principally engaged in the refining or manufacture of TNT.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
Use both terms.
A purpose-built triangulation point used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
A place of worship for members of the Methodist Reform Church. This group was the result of a secession from the Methodists in 1849. They remained until joining with the Wesleyan Association in 1857.
A place of worship for members of the Seventh Day Adventists Church. This was formed in 1843 by followers believing in the imminent second coming of Christ.
A place of worship for members of the United Methodists Church, a group formed in 1907 by the amalgamation of the United Methodist Free Church, the Methodist New Connection and the Bible Christians.

A place of worship for members of the United Methodist Free Church. Formed in 1857 by the amalgamation of the Methodist Reform Church and the Wesleyan Association they later became part of the United Methodist Church in 1907.
A place of meeting and worship for Jehovahs Witnesses.
An area of land, with associated buildings and targets, used for practicing the dropping of bombs and other aspects of air warfare.
A henge which contains a circle of standing stones. Use both terms.
Reformatory established under the Inebriates Acts 1879-1900 for repeat alcohol related offenders
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Reform Union, a movement formed in 1859 by those members of the Methodist Reform Church who did not join the Wesleyan Association.

Planned &/or landscaped areas designed for aesthetic or recreational purposes. Includes all sites, buildings, structures & features normally associated with parks & urban spaces including street furniture.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the practice of rituals & religious beliefs, including funerary rites. Includes ancillary buildings, structures & features of uncertain use, which are thought to be â€˜ritualâ€™ (eg. hill figures).
Buildings and structures associated with the performance of musical, oratory and dance events.
A stone which has a socket for an unknown function. Use specific term where known.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Bridgettine order.
A site where weapons and/or explosives are tested experimentally, or are routinely tested as part of a manufacturing quality control process.
A system of trenches dug by troops for practice purposes.

A factory used for the production of artificial limbs. They were often located within the precincts of a hospital, to enable fittings to take place and help the amputee to get used to wearing the limb.
Garden comprising rockwork features including grottoes, cascades and arches, often in different architectural styles ie. Gothic, Chinese and rustic. In use from the mid C18.

A strategic food store, directly operated by, or on behalf of, the government. The stores were used to store a variety of foodstuffs. They were in operation from the end of the Second World War until the early 1990's.
A factory for the production of missiles
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting weapons with a larger calibre ammunition such as the QF 3.75 inch (94mm) gun.
Forms of ride which are designed for entertainment.
A range marker allowing bombers to locate the bombing range.
A hospital where people would pay a subscription in order to recieve treatment when ill.

A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific from mid 1980's to early 1990's.
A barn which is constructed with a timber framework; between the members are panels which are infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brickwork, stone or other materials.
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A covered way or passage especially in a cathedral or monastic church, leading east from the cloisters between transept and chapter house.

A small prefabricated, reinforced concrete structure manufactured by Messrs Orlit Ltd for the Royal Observer Corps.  The first were ordered in 1951, most were redundant by 1955, a few remained in use in eastern England until 1965.

A small underground chamber from where it was intended to monitor radioactive fallout in the event of nuclear attack.  The majority were built between 1956 and 1964, although construction continued into the early 1970s.
Use both terms
A mechanism through which crude coal gas is passed to remove any impurities eg Ammonia and Sulphur.
A pair of SHEER LEGS mounted on shore or on a SHEER HULK, used as a crane to hoist a mast and lower it into place on a ship.
A hoist suspended from a girder within the roof of a building or workshop.

A crane consisting of a lattice girder carried on a lattice tower forming a T-shaped structure. A hoist is carried along the girder by a 'crab', enabling the crane to perform a variety of tasks eg loading/unloading of ships.
A building with an aisle on one side only.
A building with an aisle along one or both sides. Usually a row of posts separates the main space from the aisle.
The remains of a vessel which has either sunk or suffered structural damage to the extent where it can no longer function.
A building or group of buildings, incorporating radio masts, built to intercept radio transmissions from enemy vessels and aircraft during WWI and WWII.

A site, incorporating radio masts, built for high-frequency direction finding of enemy vessels and aircraft based on the interception of radio transmissions. Originally established during the First World War they were again used during the Second World War.
A firm beach or foreshore used for landing and loading of ships and other vessels. In more recent times hards have been reinforced with concrete.
A structure used for the transmission and interception of radio signals. Usually composed of a number of different elements such as aerials, receiving equipment and supporting pylons.
A site or structure associated with the activities of the Royal Observer Corps. The Corps was reformed on 1 January 1947 and disbanded in 1991.

A high status, walled, Roman burial ground containing cremations and/or inhumations in mausolea, tombs, barrows, coffins or cists. Dating from the late 1st to the 4th Century AD. DO NOT USE for cemeteries of later dates which are walled.
A one or two storey reinforced concrete structure, usually associated with two T shaped radio masts. Term is specific to army anti-aircraft control centres operational between 1950-55.
A ditch associated with a palisade.
A structure, building or room within a building, used by a local authority for the continuance of local government in the event of a military or civil emergency.
An observation post for a naval officer in charge of a marine minefield.
A site, including buildings and structures, from which communication signals are transmitted.
The sorting department of a paper factory.
A building used as a headquarters and reporting centre for an Army, Navy or Air Force Group.

The rarest of the recognized types of round barrow, consisting of a flat, wide circular mound, which may be surrounded by a ditch. They occur widely across southern England with a marked concentration in East and West Sussex.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific late 1950's to early 1970's.

A structure, often sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Sub RSGs were introduced between the RSGs and local authorities to allow the RSGs to focus on strategic direction.
A dump for wasters; pieces of pottery spoiled in the manufacturing process.
A building used for broadcasting radio programmes for public entertainment. Often includes recording studios, transmitters and offices. Use RADIO STATION for non-broadcasting uses eg. Military.

Sites, buildings, structures & features categorized by their form rather than their function, where this has been deemed to be useful for retrieval purposes. Careful consideration will be given to the inclusion of new terms within this class.
A building where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
Use only for features assumed to be archaeological but which cannot be identified more precisely without further investigation .Use more specific term where known
A structure which can be an area within a building, a separate building within a complex or a detached architectural component of a building
An area of the floor, wall or ceiling of a building, which has been painted, carved, sculpted or decorated.
An obstruction, usually manmade, which is used to restrict or prevent access to a settlement, building or area of land. Use more specific type where known.
A market consisting of stalls erected in the street and selling a variety of goods.
A warehouse used for the storage of fruit and/or vegetables.

An anti aircraft battery armed with 3 inch rockets with a ceiling of 22,000 feet. Both single and multiple launchers were designed. Single launchers being used to defend vulnerable points such as coastal batteries with multiple launchers defending town.
A searchlight battery, which points out to sea, used to locate enemy shipping
A large bath used for Jewish ritual ceremonies.
A column, in the form of a female figure, used to support an entablature.

A large room, similar to a dormitory, within a hospital, and used for the temporary or permanent accommodation of patients, either waiting for or recovering from operations or undergoing long term treatment.
An area within a hospital where children are accommodated during the period of their medical or surgical treatment.
A large room within a hospital set aside for emergency patients.
An area within a hospital where patients receiving privately-funded medical and surgical treatment are accommodated. Often includes separate rooms.
An area within a hospital where patients with contagious diseases are isolated from the rest of the hospital.
A building used by an association of persons for social and recreational purposes or for the promotion of some common object.
A room or building used as a store, usually for documents, works of art, books etc.
A residence for military personnel.
A residence for a member of a religious community eg. Abbot, Prior, Manciple etc. For multiple occupancy use more specific term eg. DORMITORY.
A house or shelter used by drovers, herders or shepherds during the seasonal moving of livestock from the highlands to the lowlands. Use more specific type where known.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for bears, including shelter. For bear baiting enclosures use BEAR PIT.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of racket sports.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of ball sports.
A building, site or structure associated with various racing sports.
An area of grass, marked out for use in the game of cricket.
A stone, slate, iron or wooden structure used to mark the site of a grave. Use only where evidence of the form is uncertain otherwise use more specific type.
Site and structures associated with the supply of clean water.
Sites and structures associated with the storage of water and waste water. Use only where the exact form or function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
Sites and structures associated with the disposal of waste water and waterborne refuse.

A reinforced concrete structure, which may be sited above ground or semi-sunken, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government from, in the event of nuclear war. Date specific to the early-mid 1950's.
Buildings and structures inhabited by agricultural workers.
A workshop used for the manufacture of statues, either cast or carved.
A factory for the manufacture of vehicles
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A workshop in which products are made using wood and timber.
An institution for the detention of prisoners, surrounded by a wall and/or fence as a barrier to escape. The level of security depends on the category of inmate detained.
An institution for the imprisonment of military personnel convicted under military law by a military court.

An institution for the imprisonment of prisoners who can be trusted to serve their sentence without likelihood of escape and of being a threat to the public. There is no physical barrier designed to prevent absconding.

An institution created with the merging of Gaols and Houses of Correction in 1865. Nowadays term used for a prison to which people are sent whilst remanded in custody before trial or direct from court after conviction.
An institution for the detention of prisoners considered to be a major threat to public safety and/or to the security of the nation.

A vertical vein of metallic ore, usually lead, occuring between walls of rock and cutting through the bedding. Often rakes have been worked from early times leaving deep trenches several km long, with adits leading off and shafts sunk at the side.
A machine in which a heavy block of metal is used for beating, breaking or driving something.
A mill used to process raw timber.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the smelting of metals.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of metal ores.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of products from metals.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of non ferrous metal ores.
A building where violins are manufactured and the art of violin making is taught.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
An air raid shelter, designed to be placed in the garden. Made from prefabricated components, they were often semi-sunken and the structure then covered with soil for added protection.
A decoy site designed to simulate the flarepath lighting of permanent RAF stations, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.
A decoy site designed to simulate permitted lighting, such as locomotives, furnaces and tramwire flashes, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
A building constructed from prefabricated sections. Use more specific type where known.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A mill in which barytes concentrates were ground to fine white powder, normally by use of flat millstones similar to those of a corn mill.
A building in which apparatus measuring the amount of water supplied/used is housed.
A structure consisting of combustible material, typically wood, on which a body is placed and then cremated, sometimes with accompanying grave goods. Use only when evidence of structure exists.
A heavy grating, often made of wood or iron, usually lowered vertically as a defensive barrier at the entrance to a gatehouse or barbican.
A building used for the safe storage and public display of jewellery, eg. the Jewel House at the Tower of London.

A factory or group of buildings engaged in the manufacture of acetone. A variety of processes may be used to manufacture acetone including the use of destructive distallation of wood and fermentation technology.
A long, narrow, rectangular plot of land used for the manufacture of rope. Usually walled, it may include small buildings and awnings at each end. Often attached to a warehouse.
A mill used for the production of wadding, as opposed to yarn or cloth. Often associated with steam or water power.
A purpose built pit, usually below a gatehouse or barbican, into which the counterweight of a drawbridge could be lowered, thus enabling the bridge to be raised.
A missile base armed with the Bristol Bloodhound surface-to-air missile. Bloodhounds were deployed to defend the launch sites of Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles.
A missile base armed with the Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile. Thor Missiles were deployed in Britain under joint British/US control between 1959 and 1964.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
A works producing gelatine from animal products for use as a culinary setting agent and in the photography, dyeing, brewing and glue industries. For explosives use GELATINE WORKS (EXPLOSIVE)
A factory used for the processing of isinglass, a product obtained from the swim bladders of sturgeon and used in the brewing industry as part of the  process for clearing wine and beer.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
A gun battery used to signal warnings to ships during bad weather.
An inn, with an integral courtyard, for the lodging and entertainment of travellers. Often with open galleried wings overlooking the courtyard.
A factory or complex of buildings where creosote oil is produced. Creosote oil is distilled from coal tar and used as a wood preservative.

A temporary structure used for the firing of bricks or tiles. Unfired bricks or tiles were stacked upon a layer of fuel (usually wood) and then surrounded by a wall of old bricks and covered by a layer of mud or clay. The clamp was then fired.
A building or site where the carcasses of whales were butchered and rendered into by products such as oil, fenk and whalebone.
A site or building where ore is processed to obtain metal.
