A flat slab of stone used to provide a level surface from which to measure the height of racehorses at a meeting, as part of the handicapping and anti fraud systems.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A building used to store fertilizers.
A building housing an economizer, a machine designed to preheat water for boilers.

A pit in a road or trackway covered with a grid, usually of metal poles (but can be of wood or stone) with sufficient space between the poles to prevent animals from crossing, without restricting access for vehicles and people.
A building or room for the storage of vegetables, particularly root vegetables, for human consumption.
A church, usually found in East Anglia, of early Medieval and/or Medieval date with attached or detached round tower.
A building or group of buildings designed for the breeding and rearing of animals, including fish and birds. Often include incubators and heated rooms.
A building, or group of buildings, deliberately designed for rhinos.
A man made terrace, often constructed in concrete, built to allow spectators a view of organized outdoor events or activities.
A barrier, usually of wood or chain, stretched across the entrance to a harbour, port or anchorage, to control entry and/or limit the effect of the weather on the wave action.
A building designed to house insects.
An enclosure for wild cats such as Lions and Tigers
A platform on which corpses are placed and allowed to decompose in the open air, so as to leave only the bones for subsequent burial.
An underground cell, or group of cells, used for imprisonment.
An underground cell, usually hidden and accessed only through a trapdoor, in which a prisoner was confined and then allegedly forgotten about.
A building used for the testing of steel.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the retrieval, refining, processing and storage of petroleum oil.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
A raised platform from which an officer can address or review his troops.
A structure indicated by the presence of post holes and of uncertain interpretation.
An institute provided by a regiment for the improvement of the soldiers and to reduce excessive drinking.
Purpose built accommodation for members of the armed forces and their families.
A trough or gutter for conveying liquids such as water or molten metal. It can be cut in the surface or formed of wood or other materials.
A purpose built section of path linking two sections of a canal enabling a horse to be led over or around an obstacle such as a hill. Horse paths predate towpath tunnels.
A canal tunnel built with one or more integral towpaths
An instrument for gauging the amount of rain which has fallen over a stated period.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which experiments and observations are undertaken to gather and record information about the weather.

A building complex, usually including kennels and cages and built close to a port or airport, in which animals can be securely held, for a designated period, to ensure that they are not carrying any infectious diseases which could be spread to others.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by sleds.
A building in which pack animals could shelter.
A marker stone erected to indicate a claim to the rights, usually mineral, of an area.
A site where cobalt is mined
A place, where a corpse could be laid whilst being carried on its way to a burial, to allow the bearers to rest.
A road, used traditionally for the transportation of a corpse to a place of burial.
An open area used for drying products manufactured using an industrial process.
A bridge in which the load is carried by a single beam, or beams, spanning the space between two supports.
A bridge, carrying a footpath or road, usually across marshy or waterlogged ground.
A type of bridge which was designed for temporary use and then capable of being moved to another site. Use for temporary bridges which have remained in situ since erection.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A bridge on which dwellings or commercial premises have been built.
A type of bridge which completely encloses the traffic using it.
A bridge whose trusses or girders form parapets on either side of the deck.
A bridge manufactured from prefabricated sections.
A bridge in which one leaf may be retracted in a horizontal plane, passing on rollers over or under the adjacent fixed leaf.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal bones.
A building used to coordinate movement of railway engines and rolling stock in the event of war.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
An installation used for the storage of ammunition.
An area of hardstanding on which ammunition is stored.
A centre attached to a prison where families and friends can visit with the inmates.
A post mill in which the drive is taken down to the base of the mill by putting an upright shaft in the hollowed post.
A plot of land longer than it is wide, can include any structures on it. Typical of medieval towns.
A building used for the preparation of animal skins and hides prior to the tanning process.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of textiles.
A pit used for the prolonged steeping of the flax plant in water to separate the fibres from the wood.
A single storey building designed so that windows incorporated into the saw tooth roof catch the available light.
A mill, on two or more levels.
A type of drying house, usually circular with a conical roof.
A loft for the drying of thread or cloth.
A workshop forming part of a domestic dwelling.
A large tank used for training divers.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.
A building complex with hangars and slipways built adjacent to a body of water where seaplanes can be stored and maintained.
A site which has been bombed but where there is no crater, eg. bombed buildings.
An old opencast iron ore site, which has been abandoned.
A mill used for the manufacture of walking sticks.
A disused term for a place where people who are physically disabled and/or have learning difficulties are cared for.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of blasing or explosive gelatine.
A building used specifically for testing the boilers of railway engines, both hydraulically and with live steam.
A maze used for the act of penitence.
A tower, consisting of one or several testing shafts, for testing lifts and for training personnel.
Workshop, as part of a gunpowder works complex, in which explosive is loaded into shells. Also used for expense magazine, where powder was stored between work processes.
Circular spoil heap surrounding a wide central depression, the entrance to a mine shaft.

A building within a gunpowder works complex, where the mill cake (pulverised and incorporated ingredients of gunpowder) was broken down. It was crushed or broken down by passing it between pairs of revolving gunmetal rollers in a breaking-down machine.

A building within the gunpowder works complex. During the gunpowder production process, the mill cake was broken down, pressed and then corned. The remaining dust was removed from the corned powder by tumbling it in gauze-covered revolving cylinders.
A component building of an explosives works where cartridges were filled with explosives with the aid of cartridging machines.

A mill which ground clinker in the cement production process. During cement production a mixture of lime and clay is burnt which forms a clinker which is then ground into powder. When mixed with water it solidifies to hard cement.
A bank, often faced with stone, with a hedge planted on top.
A clamp in which alum shale was burnt in the initial stage of processing.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A post box mounted on a lamp post.
A post box mounted in, or on, a wall.
A structure, into which a cart can be drawn, to enable it to be loaded from above.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, used for the storage of military vehicles.
A mine used for the extraction of uranium bearing ores.
A site and associated buildings used by the military for various purposes. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
The course or channel of a river or stream preserved as a geological feature.
An installation used to store ammunition and equipment ready for the mobilization of armed forces in the event of a war.
A racing track, often within a permanent stadium, for racing dogs, usually greyhounds and whippets.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
A building, usually part of a textile mill complex, where warp yarn is sized prior to weaving. Sizing is the application of a starch solution to warp threads to add strength and protection.
A manufacturing site producing weaving shuttles for the textile industry.
A building or buildings where electronic components or devices are designed, developed, manufactured and assembled.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A law court builidng established during the 1970's accommodating offices and courtrooms fro the Crown and County Courts.
A local civil court first established during the 17th Century by local Acts of Parliament to deal with minor cases of debt. Based on a model established during the reign of Henry VII.
A building housing court rooms and associated offices and cells, in which the Quarter Sessions were held.
A court of summary jurisdiction formally recognized by statute in 1848. Renamed Magistrates Court, following legislation, in 1949.
A magistrates court sitting for the purpose of holding trials for children and young people. Replaced the juvenile court, following legislation, in 1991.
A distinctive magistrates court established by legislation in 1980, dealing with civil family proceedings.
A building or complex in which visitors to a prison can meet with the inmates under the supervision of the prison staff.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in shoe making.
A factory where packaging products, such as cardboard boxes, are produced.
Container for the storage of unspecified materials.
A large, vertical revolving wheel with passenger cars or pods on the periphery used to give a bird's eye view of the surrounding area.
An area of ground which has been cleared of plants and other obstruction.
An open flat gound where the sport of shooting with bow and arrows is pursued. The ground can be equipped with targets mounted on butts and various fixed distance marker.
A military dining room where members of the armed forces eat and take recreation.
A recreation ground with usually permanent structure. It usually contains rides such as ghost trains, helter skelter and roller coasters.
The premises of a coal merchant where coal and other kinds of solid fuel can be bought.
A complex of buildings with the purpose of providing and storing food and drink supplies (esp. for the navy).
An artificial pond or pool constructed for the purpose of watering  livestock, particularly in prehistory.
A building with small observation ports used for plotting mines dropped by parachute.
An open pit from which coprolites or phosphatic nodules were extracted. Commonly found in the Fens and East Anglia coprolites were ground up and used as fertilizer.
A man-made passageway, which is built through a sea- or riverbed.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A structure used to test the aerodynamics of aircraft or vehicles.
An alignment of posts or postholes of unknown function
An alignment of stakes or stakeholes of unknown function
An alignment of trees planted as part of a designed landscape. For a belt lining a road use TREE AVENUE.
A group of trees planted as part of a designed landscape.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
A building or site used in the production of enamelled goods.
A building or site used in the production of japanned goods. Japanning was the process of covering a material with a hard, black lacquer in imitation of Japanese lacquer work.
A building or site for the industrial manufacture of locks.
A kiln used for extracting salt through the evaporation of salt water.
A site used for the extraction of peat.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
An area speciallly developed to accommodate commercial buildings.

A stone faced earth bank, usually with a concave batter, and with the base the same width as its height and the top half the width of the base.  Vegetation usually grows out of the top.  Found mainly in Cornwall, but also elsewhere in the Atlantic Arc.
A boat roofed over and fitted up as a home for living in permanently or temporarily.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include  three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.
A group of electricity-producing windmills or wind turbines.
An apparatus designed with a large vaned wheel rotated by the wind in order to generate electricity.
A building or compound housing a permanent establishment of members of a religious organization to do missionary work.
Area of land set aside and managed for the preservation of flora, fauna, their natural habitats and physical features.
Garden or open-air enclosure, usually connected to commercial premises, where tea and other refreshments are served to the public.
House, where destitute Jews converted to Christianity after the expulsion. Latin for House of Converts.""

A decorative emblem stating the name of a village or town and depicting aspects of the place's history of culture. Most signs are mounted on a post and usually errected in a central position near the church or village green.
Shelter on military airfield to provide night time accommodation for airmen during WWII.

A facility where natural gas is made smaller in volume, to facilitate its distribution through the National Transmission System. Term can also be used for a station, which recompresses the gas to the required pressure.
A building or other establishment used for the retail, making and repairing of jewellery.
A government employment agency for those out of work offering advice on jobs, training and retraining.
In Roman architecture either 1. A block of buildings enclosed by four streets or 2. A large tenement house or apartment block.
Starshaped cairn with three radial arms of equal length, a monument unique to upland Northumberland. (Late Neolithic or early Bronze Age).
The residence or official premises of a consul, the official appointed by a state to protect its citizens and commercial interests in a foreign state.
A building or buildings used for the production of pens.
A building or buildings used for the production of whistles.
A route across a river, or lake. Use only for small inland ferries and index with LANDING POINT/STAGE/STEPS or PIER where known.

Part of the WWII air defence radar system, whereby in 1939 a chain of radar stations were established along the south and east coast of Britain. The equipment was based upon apparatus developed for ionospheric research.
A raised platform or stage for public speaking or conducting an orchestra. Also a platform for supporting cameras during filming.
A foreshore structure to prevent barges from sinking in the river mud. Made by placing chalk on fascines of brushwood, which is in some cases retained by a timber revetement.
A sports arena with a steeply banked oval track for bicycle racing. There are outdoor as well as indoor velodromes.
An enclosed area of land of varying size and shape which shows traces of defence.
A position or place that allows a wide or favourable overall view of a scene or situation.
Term applied to both the pit trap itself, and the walled enclosure containing pit trap(s).

Standard dwelling of the non-ruling classes of Japan until the mid twentieth century. Minkas are timber-framed houses with mud-plastered panels and thatched roofs. The design varies from region to region. Minkas served as home as well as workplace.
A shop housing the business of a grindery dealer. Grindery are the tools and materials used by shoemakers and other leather-workers.
A track of two parallel ruts deliberately cut in the ground or living rock for the guidance of two-wheeled carts when the way was obscured by darkness or water.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted under ground.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted.

An offshore station, equipped with a fixed electronic radio navigation and positioning system such as Hyperfix. The transmission principle are pulsed and phase comparisons systems. Superceded by Global Positioning System in 1994.
A piece of forest land converted into arable.
Buildings and structures associated with the processing and storage of natural gas.
A boat, ship or other vessel either whole or in part. Watercraft often survive as commemorative monuments or have been reused as floating restaurants, museums, hotels etc.
An area off the coast where ships anchor.
A boiling vessel used in the direct boiling process, or the sleeching process, used for the manufacture of salt. For evaporating features associated with SOLAR and PARTIAL SOLAR sites use SALT POND.
A depot or warehouse for the storage, distribution and repair of shoe making machines.
A 19th century structure of various shape or material for the protection of troops in an emergency.
A type of large steel framed aircraft hangar introduced by the Royal Air Force in its Expansion Period with a number of designs between 1934 and 1939, to accomodate heavy bombers.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
Use Grinding House for a place material is crushed and Grindery for a place where metal objects are sharpened.
A place where two artificial waterways meet each other.
Site associated with the testing of nuclear material or its containers.
A building or site used for the production of frameworks of beds.
A site which has produced evidence of in situ production of items derived from antler.
A trench dug in order to receive the foundations of a structure such as a stone wall etc.
A pit filled with rubble, etc., into which rain or waste water flows in order to disperse into the surrounding soil.

A type of temporary military aircraft hangar introduced in 1940; of steel welded and bolted construction typically clad in galvanized corrugated iron sheets. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF in World War Two.

A type of military building associated with military airfields, where air crews were briefed for missions. The room could be a seperate building or part of an operations block and are built of varying types of temporary brick or nissen hut constructions.
A chamber attached to the sewer of a building to facilitate the removal of any blockage.

A type of transportable aircraft hangar patented by Miskins and Sons in 1939. The arched hangar was constructed of steel or wooden ribs and generally clad in steel sheets. The hangar did not require any foundations and could be anchored by iron stakes.
A slaughterhouse for horses.

A large type of military repair hangar mainly used on WWII bomber bases, constructed using steel stanchions and clad in corrugated iron. B 1 hangars were part of a series of prefabricated buildings intended to supplement existing hangars on bases.
A building of varying designs intended for directing military aviation operations. Normally associated with military airfields.

A type of steel framed transportable British military aircraft hangar developed from 1941onwards. The hangar had a steel frame, some versions used commercially available sheeting for cladding. It was similar to but smaller than the arcraft hangar type T2.

A building that houses material that can be used to facilitate the study of a site, landscape or an historical event/period. Such centres are often found in close proximity to the sites and/or landscapes that they seek to encourage the study of.
A type of temporary transportable aircraft hangar designed in 1936 by N.S. Bellman. It was designed for ease of installation, and was composed of light rolled steel sections.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a naval dockyard.
A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.
A camp for the temporary accommodation of uprooted civilians or foreign ex-service personnel, who had fought for the British forces during WWII (e.g.Polish).

A circular or octagonal building at the base of a post mill to provide storage space and to give protection to the superstructure. The roundhouse is not attached to the mill itself. Some roundhouses were later converted for domestic purposes.

A permanent military RAF aircraft hangar type, designed in 1924. It features a steel frame (with longitudinal ridge and valley trusses for the roof) reinforced concrete and brick infilling for the walls. Typically 122 foot span by 249 foot in length.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, some examples have steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
Early name for aircraft hangar (up until around 1940), when the term hangar was only used for a tent construction.
Early name for aircraft hangar (ca. up until 1940), when the term hangar was only used for a tent construction.
A place where dead animals are buried.
A pit where calcium oxide (Quicklime) has been hydrated to produce calcium hydroxide, known as slaked lime.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, one example has steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
A mill where china stone is grinded.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of crucibles.

A large steelframed military aircraft hangar designed in 1939, intended for aircraft maintenance on operational stations. It includes side annexes for workshops and offices, provided with a large number of windows. The annexes are of brick or concrete.
Hut along the coast, which provided shelter for lookouts, known as huers, who kept watch for the pilchard shoals that passed by the coast. Built of stone or wood. Particular common to Cornwall.
A wall structure built to direct a current into the desired channel in a harbour, river etc.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphate is extracted.

Building block (often a temporary brick structure or Nissen hut) comprising office accommodation for flight commanders and flight sergeants as well as pilots' rest rooms, storerooms and locker rooms. Some flight offices have central corridors.

A curved military aircraft hangar produced in 1939. The frame is steel which is then clad with steel sheeting and reinforced concrete and typically covered with a thin layer of concrete, earth and turf.

The first transportable aircraft hangar developed by the RFC/RAF, which comprised a kit of timber and canvas that could be assembled in 48 hours. The canvas doors open one end only. Also known as Type H hangar.

A mill for the processes of grinding, balling, couching, drying and packing of woad. The mill can be demountable, enabling it being located close to the fields, as woad crop has to be rotated and move to new fields as soon as the ground is exhausted.
Site where fossils where mined for use as artificial fertilizer. Use both terms
Saxon rectangular burial chamber comprising a large sunken 'room' lined with wood. 6th and 7th century AD.
A surface interpreted as a buried cultivation layer, for example an agriculturally cultivated field.
A steel framed transportable hangar similar in construction to Type T2 but about half the size. Designed in 1941 and 1942.
A widening in a canal to allow boats to turn around.

Accommodation given rent-free along with or as part of a corrody, which is a provision of an annual allowance of food and money by a religious house to an individual, usually in return for service or by purchase. Term used until mid 16th century AD.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows an almost rectangular course.

Medieval Fenland ditched field system where the land is divided into strips for agricultural production. The strips are separated by hand-dug wide shallow drainage ditches with the spoil thrown up to create a dryer ridge.
Term used in particular in Lincolnshire instead of Darland Field System.
An inhumation burial in which the corpse is laid on a wooden bed, often surrounded by a collection of grave-goods. Anglo-Saxon rite of 7th century AD.
An area of agriculturally used land, which is divided into small, elongated, rectangular fields running parallel to each other.
A small concrete turret placed on top of a standard 4 ft. diameter concrete pipe sunk into the ground. Intended for use in defending road junctions, airfields and beach exits.
The limit line of an area pertaining to a medieval manor.
The limit line of a medieval local administrative unit of a hundred.

A type of aircraft hangar from the closing years of WWI either of steel or wood utilising a type of lattice work roof support known as a Belfast Truss, which features diagonally interlaced pieces of thin pine. The roof appears as a smooth curve.

A modern building system in which both steel and concrete are utilized together to carry the load in ways that neither material predominates over the other. There are many varieties e. g. a steel frame surrounding a concrete core.
A covered passageway projecting into or across a ditch of a fortified place to provide flanking fire to the ditch in which it stands or for the purpose of sheltering communication with outworks.

A signalling structure used on WWII airfields, comprising a concrete square base with a kerbed border into which concrete signal symbols could be placed to advise pilots in the air of current airfield state e.g. directions of landing and airfield circuit.
Large concrete letters representing the ground-to-air airfield code. It has been used to show pilots in WWII the name of the airfield they were above e.g. DW for Dunkeswell.

An airfield building housing a turret gunnery trainer used to teach air gunners how to report the correct position of enemy aircraft by practising shooting against projected moving images of enemy aircraft displayed on a target screen (WWII).
Building or buildings housing  equipment for generating heat for a building complex.
An aircraft maintenance workshop deriving from the use of  weather proofing varnish to aircraft canvas called dope in order to keep the canvas taut and airtight. From 1912 onwards.""

A large circular defence work surrounded by a brick revetted ditch and sunken below a glacis. Usually built out of brick with the embrasures lined with granite blocks. Armed with ten or elven guns. Early 19th century as part of coastline defence.
A housing estate comprised of housing stock owned and let by a local authority.
A building housing machinery for crushing chalk for whiting. Whiting was used in toothpaste, paint, tablets, putty and other products.
A ground used for the performance testing of motor vehicles, for example prototype vehicles.
A defence work, either a detached fieldwork or an outwork built as part of a fortification as a last defensive position.

In fortification, a detached triangular outwork consisting of two battered faces forming a salient angle. Usually positioned in the ditch in front of a rampart and between two bastions. Term mainly for military architecture from 15th century and later.
Use for the remains of a cargo which have been accidentally lost at sea, or purposefully dumped, and which consist the only physical evidence of a vessel.
A building housing washing facilities and toilets. The term occurs mainly in a military context.

Buildings used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for buildings associated with military installations. For non-military, use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.

A land based installation armed with wire -guided and powered  Brennan torpedoes which were in operation beween 1890 and 1906. These torpedoes were invented by Louis Philip Brennan. The stations were used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.""
A building housing material used to explain the significance of a site or landscape to the public e. g. an archaeological site or nature reserve.
A type of 1930s civillian aircraft hangar comprising a large gabled building  with a mild steel structure and asbestos cladding.
A defensive construction situated in the sea, designed to protect the land from seabourne attack. The term applies mainly to those monuments built from around 1860 onwards.
A component of a salt works housing iron pans where the brine was evaporated above a furnace and flue. Such houses were lightly built in order to allow the heat and steam to escape.

A structure consisting of different cells equipped with instrument posts which supported finders. These provided range and bearing of the projected position of the target to guns emplaced in a nearby battery. Errected along the coast in the late 1870s.

A small dispersal WWII military aircraft hangar featuring an A shaped steel frame clad with corrugated iron; end doors were supported by outriggers when open.Typically used on aircraft storage units or satellite landing grounds. Variations in size.""
Sites, buildings or stuctures associated with the entire process of salt production.
A component of salt works containing flues and drying areas where salt blocks are dried before being crushed and bagged.

A type of large permanent military aircraft hangar with a curved steel frame and storage annexes on its side used in World War II. It was intended for storage purposes on Aircraft Storage Unit stations.

A building or part of a building, sometimes attached to a religious community, where religious activities such as worshipping, meetings, teaching about the faith and conferences take place. It can also provide accommodation.

An artificially constructed wall with recessed and projecting grips for hands and feet and places to attach ropes. Used for practising rock climbing. If the wall is situated within a sports centre use term from Components thesaurus.

A sunken, circular, concrete pillbox used on airfields. They remained flush with the surface to permit the free movement of aircraft but, if attack threatened, could be raised hydraulically or by a counterbalance, and manned to give covering fire.

A type of military aircraft hangar of the Cold War, hardened and therefore protected against the effects of nuclear weapons. It comprises a semi-circular structure built of corrugated-steel supporting a reinforced-concrete skin. Three NATO designs.
Buildings and structures associated with a private aviation club undertaken as a leisure pursuit. Usually situated on or near an airfield.
A military side-opening aircraft hangar originally designed for seaplanes and used RNAS bases from 1916. Steel framed with asbestos or corrugated iron cladding.
A building or site where aircraft can be stored and maintained.

Headquarters buildings on military airfields for administrative purposes housing offices, lecture rooms and in some cases a library and a meteorological office. On smaller airfields it is called Station Offices. Abbreviation SQH.
A military storage aircraft hangar built  in the late 1930s. It comprises a semicircular concrete structure with reinforced concrete columns, featuring a curved roof and straight walls.
A military storage aircraft hangar designed in 1937. It has a curved profile and is constructed from steel ribs supporting a concrete skin. The roof is covered with earth and turf.
A special school to train personnel for employment in Air Traffic Control and operation duties.

A supermarket for American military personnel, the National Guard and the Reserves and their immediate family, usually sited on a military installation throughout the world. Use term only in conjunction with an American military base.
A prepared area used for the game of baseball.

A steel aircraft hangar evolved from the German Lamellendach, a segmental roof design of the 1920s using a diamond shaped web of pressed steel producing a hangar with a shallow curving profile. Used for both military and civil purposes.

A short-term storage centre of goods or special parts to facilitate the rapid processing of orders and supply of goods to customers; unlike a warehouse, the emphasis is on the moving of goods rather than on a long-term storage.
A mutiple role hangar for aircraft and general storage, manufactured in the USA as a kit for on-site assembly  during WWII and post-war. It comprises a steel box frame and a canvas covering.
A steel framed seaplane hangar designed for Royal Navy Air Stations by the admiralty in 1917-1918.
An area on post-war military airfields for parking aircraft on quick reaction alert to allow immediate access to the runway. Abbreviation ORP.
A device on an airfield for securing aircrafts when parked outside in order to prevent major movement due to the weather or other conditions.
An aircraft hangar designed to be moved from site to site as necessary.
A temporary, steel-framed transportable hangar developed by Teesside Bridge and Engineering Company to replace the obsolete Bellman hangars.

A transportable hangar designed by Callender Cable and Construction to Air Ministry drawing number 6633/37. A steel box-girder framework with corrugated iron cladding and canvas doors it had a clear door height of 25ft.
A small arched hangar built by the Canadian company Fromson of Byfleet to drawing number 3971/43. Used only as storage sheds on RNASs.
A transportable hangar designed by A & J Main of Glasgow.
An all-steel end-opening, hangar with canted sides designed for folded-wing aircraft.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design number 454/43. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes
Aircraft hangars designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers to meet the requirement to repair damaged heavy bombers in situ on their airfields.
An aircraft hangar designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers usually erected on aircraft factory sites rather than operational airfields.
A single-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich (drawing number 4178/44). Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
A double-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich. Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
A semi-permanent ahed designed to Air Ministry specification 1136/27 as a quick and cheap hangar for stations overseas
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specification (drawing number 6910/43). Similar in design to the ROBINS AIRCRAFT HANGAR but larger.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specifications (drawing number 2243/41). Constructed from prefabricated A-frames and clad in corrugated iron.
An aircraft hangar designed to house seaplanes.
A side-opening steel framed shed. A smaller version of the SEAPLANE SHED (TYPE F) they were built from 1916 on RNAS seaplane bases
A watch office designed for bomber satellite station comprising a long, temporary brick hut with a watch office, operations room and crew briefing room.

A detached building without an operations block and crew briefing room designed on modern lines similar to, but smaller than WATCH OFFICE (12779/41). Began appearing on new stations from September 1941.

A central tower with a single-storey wing either side. The tower contained the watch office on the ground floor, observation room on the second with each wing containing an office for the Chief Flying Instructor or the officer commanding and their aides.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the Air Ministry. Usually found on or near airfields.
A site or building associated with active or passive defence of the landing ground and buildings of an airfield.
A pillbox constructed for use in training exercises forming part of a simulated defensive position
A pillbox in which the roof is detached from the walls and supported by a central pillar, thus leaving an embrasure allowing a 360 degree field of fire.
A pillbox which has been modified from a standard Directorate of Fortifications and Works design. Double index with specific type where known.
A construction designed to look like a pillbox in order to deceive or confuse the enemy.
A pillbox constructed of prefabricated concrete panels. Double index with specific type where known.
A pillbox with walls that have been thickened to protect against shells. Double index with specific type where known.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of South-Eastern Command.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.

A circular pillbox, usually consisting of a concrete pipe with a timber and corrugated iron roof, surrounded and covered by earth and sandbags. Built to a design by Norcon Ltd, a company dealing in concrete pipes.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers in Southern Area (Taunton Line).
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.
A pillbox built to a design by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.

A hexagonal pillbox, with an internal anti-ricochet wall and loopholes for fives light machine guns and one rifle. Originally designed to have 15in bulletproof walls many were built with 42in thick shellproof walls. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting smaller, faster weapons such as Bofors guns or a single anti-aircraft machine gun, intended to engage fast low flying aircraft.

A hexagonal pillbox with an interanl anti-ricochet wall. The rear wall was lengthened to take two rifle loopholes in addition to the five light machine gun. Both 15in and 42in thick walls are common. Designed by DFW branch 3.

A circular pillbox designed by the Engineering and Metals Company using 'Armco' corrugated iron sheets as the inner and outer skins into which concrete was poured, giving a 12in wall thickness. The design was taken up by DFW and assigned a drawing number.

A square pillbox with loopholes for four light machine guns with 18 in thick walls. Probably designed by DFW branch 3 although it may have been adapted from an external source as Southern Command correspondence refers to the type as 'Stento'.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.

A square pillbox with walls up to 48in thick, designed to emplace a 2 pounder anti-tank gun. A large opening in the back allowed the gun to be wheeled into position at the large embrasure in the front wall. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A defensive structure or site where an anti-tank gun is emplaced.
A large, rectangular pillbox based on the FW3/28 with the addition of a small infantry chamber to one side of the main gun chamber.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.
A pillbox which varies from standard designs.
A machine gun post designed by James Ruck constructed from hollow blocks and prefabricated concrete sheeting with loopholes allowing for a garrison of eight.
A rotating, domed, steel turret set over a circular pit used as a gun emplacement.
A flatbed lorry with a concrete defensive position fitted on the back enabling the pillbox to be driven to where it was most needed in the event of an airborne force landing on the airfield.""
The first standardized design for a building for the duty pilot. It took the form of a small bungalow with a bay window on the front elevation.
A small single storey structure with just one room containing a pyrotechnic cupboard and built of rendered brick with a flat reinforced concrete roof
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 14383/40.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 17658/40.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 18441/40.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 3156/41.
A two storey building with a watch office on the ground floor and a control room above. Originally based on drawing number 12096/4.
A night fighter station watch office based on the standard design dor Bomber Satellite Station watch offices

TERM: ROYAL NAVAL AIR STATION CONTROL TOWER
SCOPE_NOTE: A control tower constructed on RNAS stations by the Royal Marine Engineers. Built to a common ground floor plan they could be built with one, two or three storeys above this depending on the requirements of the station.
A three-storey RNAS control tower, incorporating meteorological office on the ground floor and an air watch office on the second floor.

A four-storey RNAS control tower. The first floor contained offices for the commander flying and meteorological offices and the upper two floors, in the form of a central tower, provided offices for air traffic control.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
Stone used for grinding or polishing during the manufacture of lithic implements
A small, single storey building used as the Pilots' room on fighter stations and as the watch office on bomber stations.

A two-storey, structure with a brick ground floor and a reinforced concrete upper floor with balcony and large windows to the watch office and control room. This became the most common building design for air traffic control in the Second World War.
A small building housing pilot's and locker rooms with flight offices and a watch office. The only known example was built at Tangmere.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34. It became the standard design for watch offices with a large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
An informal encampment, usually near a military establishment, set up as a public protest against that establishment or against some aspect of military policy.
A building where advice and aid appertaining to physical and economic wellbeing of disadvantaged members of a community are made available.
An establishment from which food is distributed to the public during wartime or similar states of emergency.
An opening or cavity through which a stream or natural watercourse disappears underground.

A secure, bomb-proof, undergound complex designed to be used by the government in the event of a national emergency such as nuclear war. Usually equipped with communications equipment, emergency rations and water and air filtering plants.
A hospital which has been built either wholly, or partially, underground in order to protect it from attacks by enemy aircraft.
A railway yard with associated buildings used for the maintenance and storage of locomotive engines and rolling stock.
A reservoir or tank used to hold a supply of water for fire-fighting purposes in the event of the main supply being damaged or cut off.
A board, wall painting or other structure displaying advice, giving information or directions
A radio station set up to broadcast signals aimed at 'bending' or altering German navigation transmissions.
A sundial capable of giving an accurate reading of standard time to the minute.
A tunnel built to allow internees (in a camp, prison etc.) to escape.
A telephone exchange housing one end of an underwater cable and used to send messages overseas.

A cable repeater station for the undersea telephone and telegraph cables. Repeater stations compensated for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.
A ditch constructed to surround a town for defensive purposes.
A small brewery, often situated in a public house, producing limited quantities of beer, for consumption locally and/or on the premises.
Stadium housing a track and associated buildings and structures for the public racing of greyhounds.

A wall within a lead mine surrounding a dressing floor, where waste from mining and smelting is deposited, to protect livestock from entering and consuming contaminated material and becoming poisoned, or 'bellanded'.
A building with a range of educational and recreational facilities for the exclusive use of its all-female membership.
A cleansing house associated with Jewish burial ceremonies
An enclosed encampment, often featuring temporary or semi-permanent structures, used for the detention of prisoners of war, refugees or other civilians detained on political or social grounds.
A place where telephones and their components are manufactured
An establishment where beauty treatments and associated therapies are provided by professional practitioners.

A horizontal surface separating the base of a rampart or earthwork from an associated ditch or moat. Can also refer to a continuously sloping bank of earth against a wall, as in a fortified city wall.
A section of roadway attached at one end to a harbour or dockside and ending at a landing stage, rising and falling with the tide, for the loading and unloading of vehicles and pedestrians.
A large area, usually open-air, used for permanent, seasonal or regular shows, events or exhibitions.
An establishment for the preparation and selling of food to be consumed off the premises.
A structure, often sunk into the ground, for the purpose of allowing total bodily immersion in mineral sprinwater or similarly beneficial substances.
An umbrella-shaped pavilion, Indian in origin, constructed over a funerary site. Can also refer to a funerary monument or cenotaph constructed in this style.
A depression in the ground caused by the impact of a falling object, such as a crashed aircraft.
Garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of the deceased are scattered or buried.
Residence for retired people, often in the form of an apartment complex, differing from a nursing home as the residents live independently.
Housing provided for refugees. Similar to refugee camp but with the reuse of existing buildings rather than a temporary camp.
Coastal base for the docking, launch and maintenance of submarines.
Part of textile mills.
A site or factory where waste slag from ironworking if further processed for use in manufacturing.
A building providing business premises to companies or individuals, sometimes for short periods, in exchange for a membership fee.
The official residence of an abbot.
A functioning clock designed to serve also as an ornamental feature or sculpture.
A prefrabicated home sited in parks where a pitch fee is charged. Although technically mobile they usually only make one journey before being permanently installed.

An unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting avtivities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools with a covering structure.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often part of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
A club where predominantly rhythm and blues style music is played, analagous to a jazz club.
Obstacles, including scaffolding and anti tank blocks designed to impede an enemy's attempts to land forces onto open beaches.
A place where a group of people live together sharing accomodation and goods, forming their own community based upon common ideals.
A building where people congregate to undertake sustained mental contemplation or religious or spiritual reflection.

Manmade structure for bathing or swimming that is located on the beachfront and filled by tidal waters. Similar to a LIDO, with the main difference being the extent of the built up complex around the pool.
A Roman market hall principally selling meat and poultry but also other provisions.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or navvys.""
A type of fairground or seaside amusement, often a permanent structure, where carriages travel at high speeds on an undulating track raised some distance from the ground.
A depot for the depositing, storage and dispatch of plant or other resources associated with the delivery of local government public services.
Seaside structure, usually consisting of a manmade retaining wall that keeps a relatively large area of the tidal water partitioned off for controlled boating or swimming.

A pit in which lye is used to clean hides/bones/etc. generally as part of the tanning process to remove excess fat, flesh, hair, etc. from the raw hide.  The residue from these pits formed a crude soap which could be used for various cleaning purposes.

A concrete structure, based on drawing number (11008/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was considered less vulnerable than the (3329/41).
A structure, often concrete or brick, used as a shelter by members of the British citizen army during watch or patrol duties, or air raids, in wartime.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
Obstacles, often semi permanent, which are placed on railway lines to prevent the enemy from using them. Set up during the defence of Britain.
Place for the Home Guard to store equipment and amunition, either structural or subterranean during the defence of Britain.
General term describing any defence work where no more specific term is applicable.
A bridge which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.
Chamber built into underside of a structure to exercise demolition.
Fixed or hardened installation for machine guns. Temporary soft installations are possible as well.
Obstacles like concrete cubes, cylinders or pimples erected in the defence of Britain.
Block, often made of concrete, to secure smaller maritime craft. Many were made during the Second Wold War to secure craft which were to be used in the D-Day landings.
A site, usually including fuel tanks, pipe works and control buildings, where flaming petroleum was intended to be used as a weapon against a hostile invasion.
A rectilinear ritual enclosure of Iron Age date
A factory used for the production of acetate.
A tall pole topped with a bell used to summon the workforce to their place of work.
A building housing the brakes for an incline railway or tramway.
A pump used for moving brine (salt water).
Use both terms
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A site associated with the large scale construction of buildings or items manufactured by the building industry.
A building or site where lead is obtained from ore.
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
A stone or timber lined channel for conveying ore out of a working.
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
Term applied to a pit trap itself and also a walled enclosure containing one or more pit traps.
A grave which has been formed by cutting into the bedrock of a site.
A chute for conveying salt.
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
A group of, usually three, standing stones forming a square with an open side and often found with a stone circle.
A site where tanks and armoured fighting vehicles can be stored.
To aid migration from RSM to IDS. DO NOT USE FOR INDEXING!
A building or site used for the manufacture of whiting either from crushed chalk, limestone, marble or through chemical preparation.
A small island, especially within a river.

An establishment originally providing terminals to allow the public to access the internet, usually for a fee. They originally provided snacks and drinks to customers although now this is not always the case.
Refers to art, whether carving or painting, applied to free -standing stones or cave walls.
Art applied in pigment to rock wether in the form of a free-standing stone or the walls of a cave.
A searchlight battery used to light a beach.
A slight structure built on an allotment for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, by the allotment holder.

Purpose-built structure, other than a bollard, to prevent vehicle or pedestrian access to a road or site, for example concrete blocks to obstruct vehicles accessing beaches on the north-east coast for illegal sea-coaling.
Fast arterial road with separate carriageways limited to motor vehicles
A circular construction at the intersection of two or more roads to aid the passage of vehicles from one road to another.
A cover consisting of a plate for covering over or closing in a chamber or receptacle.
An iron cover for a manhole
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
A tower with one or more horizontal platforms extending out over deep water for use in diving competitions.
The site of the formal burial of cremated bone, sometimes 'urned' in a vessel or casket of glass, wood or, more commonly, ceramic.
An intrusive feature cut for the purpose of containing a cremation burial within it.
A kitchen set up, specifically during World War Two, to serve food to members of the public, especially families whose homes had succumbed to enemy bombing.
An area of privately owned land attached to, and incorporating, a country house and associated buildings.
A structure providing protection from the elements to passengers waiting to board a ferry service at a dock, riverside, harbour or quay.
A linear groove worn into the surface of a road or thoroughfare by the continuous passage of wheeled vehicles. Usually expected to occur in pairs.
A tank found on hop farms in which creosote was held, heated from below by a fire with a chimney. The ends of hop poles were dipped in the tar to prevent rotting in soil.
A hut provided as accommodation for hop pickers and may also be know as a Hop Pickers' Hut
For funerary monuments use CATACOMB (FUNERARY), for wine use WINE CELLAR
A building used as the headquarters for the Home Guard during the Second World War.
A workshop or factory unit where small or light goods are manufacture without the need for large-scale industrial machinery.
An area, with fixed defences, designed to act as a focal point for a defending force.
Sites, buildings and structures associated with the prevention of an invasion by a hostile force.
A designated area, usually sited at a strategic crossroads, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to act as a rallying point for defenders.
A fortified river or river bank forming part of the anti invasion infrastructure.
A well concealed structure, usually constructed underground, intended for use by members of the British Resistance Organization in the event of invasion.
An anti-personnel device consisting of a 40 gallon fuel drum placed on top of an explosive charge and detonator. When detonated the barrel would explode sending burning fuel over the intended target.

Name given to a workhouse after 1929. The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished Poor Law Unions and Guardians, and control passed to public assistance authorities run by county boroughs and county councils. Lasted until 1948 when poor laws were repealed.
A decoy site designed to simulate a burning urban area during a bombing raid in order to lure enemy bombers away from legitimate targets.
A deposit that has been burnt and not subsequently disturbed. Refer to Archaeological Science thesaurus for terminology relating to those redeposited from their original location.
A construction trench dug to receive a line of posts for a wall, with associated packing.
A tunnel with strengthened construction, used as an emergency exit from a civil defence building.
A hearth constructed specifically for the manufacture of pitch.
A former ground surface buried beneath an earthwork or other sequence of deposits. (includes palaeosoils, turf lines)
Debris consisting of excess construction material used in the building of a nearby site or structure. If unsure of whether debris is from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
Debris derived from the demolition of buildings or other structures. If unsure of whether debris is resulting from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
A privately-funded home for the care of the elderly.
Mark, usually consisting of a horizontal line above an arrow, cut by the Ordnance Survey as part of the survey of Britain and referenced to a known height above mean sea level.
A stone, of unidentified function, showing evidence of great heating at some point in the past, leading to vitrification.
A concrete marker placed to indicate the direction of a target on a bombing range to aircraft.
An enclosed observation tower, usually made of brick or concrete and raised on four legs, associated with WW2 bombing ranges.
A store for hay, at a remove from the farm (Scots)
Residence of a leading land-holding family within the district.
Cluster of dwellings of medieval or later date (Scots)
A pit used to trap game. Often originally covered and consealed, and sometimes with sharpened stakes in the base.
Temporary accommodation for war evacuees.
A building or settlement enclosure with a thick drystone wall, generally circular or oval in plan, usually sited in an elevated position.
A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.

An Iron Age round defended house, found mainly in the north and west of Scotland. Brochs have a tapering profile and thick, usually hollow dry stone walls which contain galleries, cells and a stairway, with guard cells at the entrance.
A factory where security safes are manufactured.
A factory for the manufacture of military tanks.
Factory or workshop making bits, spurs and other small metal objects associated with horse harness.

A purpose-built facility providing an area for wheeled sports, such as skateboarding, skating and BMX cycling, equipped with ramps and other structures and obstacles for the performance of tricks and manoeuvres.
A mill for producing abravive papers and cloths such as glass paper or emery cloth.
A mill for grinding ochre for the paint making process.
A camping place set aside for the use of caravans.
A purpose built indoor cricket facility for training and playing matches
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
An outdoor trail that has keep fit equipment with supporting information plaques intermittently positioned along its route
A prepared piece of ground on which the game of Petanque is played.
A site used for the butchery of animals.
Fairground attraction designed to create optical illusions to give a sense of unbalance and unease.
Fairground attraction containing a number of ghoulish displays designed to scare visitors.
A building containing soft play equipment for children.

A pass, vulnerable to attack from the enemy but essential for the movement of troops and which, if captured, could divide a defending force. As a result such passes are defended with anti invasion defences such as pillboxes.
An area, often a village, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to stop the advance of an enemy force and to hold out for an agreed period of time.
Purpose built or modified structure used for scenery in a film.
A suburb of a town, especially Roman or Medieval, situtated or extending beyond its formal limits, usually demarked by defences.
Purposely built camp with recreational facilities and individual chalets for accommodation.

Rocket projector site with a circular or octagonal concrete holdfast, 1.5m across, surrounded by a 4.6m radius octagonal concrete surround. Six such rocket projectors were arranged in a 3 x 2 grid. Personnel shelters placed midway between each site.
64 Type DFW55373 projector sites arranged in and 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
6 DFW55373 projector emplacements spaced in a 3x2 rectangular gid, but each spaced 35m apart. No blast protection was provided at the shelters, which were placed between the projector emplacements.

Unspecified Second World War anti-aircraft battery. There were three types of battery. The U2P and U20P had different arrangements of DFW55373 projector sites for the 20-barrelled 3 projectors. The U9P mounted 12-barrelled projectors.
A plinth or pedestal, usually of concrete, to which an anti aircraft or coastal battery gun was fitted. Holdfasts are often the only evidence for a weapon which survive.
A centre in which the public donate blood that will be used for the care of patients in hospitals.
A site in which one or more searchlights and their accompanying structures were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
64 Type DFW55373 single projector sites arranged in an 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
Range used by the Navy with reinforced observation huts which housed quadrant equipment to record accuracy and damage.
A building used in the Second World War to co-ordinate action against enemy air raids.
A roomspace within an abode which combines the specific functions of several of the more traditional roomspaces into a singular unified space.
Second World War defence work usually consisting of securinng points for a boom defence, associated gun, and searchlight, emplacements
Buildings and structures used to monitor the accuracy of bombs dropped on a bombing range
A centre used by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A storage facility used for the accommodation and dispersal of vehicles. Often used by the military and emergency services.
Beaches used for the departure of troops and equipment for the D-day landings.

Special concrete loading ramps nicknamed 'hards' had been constructed along river banks, beaches and inlets to enable organised embarkation onto various types of landing craft to take place, irrespective of tides.
Site or building constructed or adapted for indoor and/or outdoor leisure and sport activities, for example archery, team-building and outward-bound activities based on military training.""
A structure, usually of earth and concrete, and usually, although not always, subterranean, designed for protection against explosives.
Non-specific building type associated with an airfield.
A picture or pattern produced by either by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours or by painting directly onto a wall.

An establishment used for the manufacture of reeds and healds, which are components of a textile loom with related functions, in that they move and control the threads, and similar wire-based construction.
An establishment used for the manufacture of jacquards and dobbys, which are textile loom components that control the weaving of complicated or figured patterns.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
A device used to remove pollutants from gas or smoke produced during industrial processes such as burning high-sulphur fuels.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
Buildings and structures associated with the acquisition of electronic signals for the purpose of intelligence gathering.
A building housing computers and information technology equippment e.g. for a business, factory or other instituion.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
School built by the local Education Authority to provide residental schooling at the seaside for children from urban communities.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores  and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
A site from which troops could be embarked onto transport vessels prior to the D-Day landings can also apply to muster/departure points from which troops embarked for their journey to the Front.

6 Type DFW 55373s placed in a 3X2 rectangular plan. Each projector was separated by 31-34m. Hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each projector, but ammunition stored outside the perimeter.
A site used by the Air Raid Precautions network. Use more specific term.
A seperate wing of a large house provide accommodation for guests.
A short or long term residential home for people not requiring medical intervention or nursing care, usually for older people.

A solid concrete or stone base on which a machine (often an engine and therefore called the engine bed, forming part of an engine house) was mounted to power an industrial process. Dates from the 19th century.
An apparatus used for the process of condensing: the conversion of vapour into a liquid.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
An industrial building, plant or site where crude substances, such as sugar, metal, oil etc., are purified or refined.
An establishment used to serve ice cream to the general public.
A building from which the firing of torpedoes can be controlled and evaluated.
A prepared area of ground, featuring a 'mini' golf course with obstacles, used to undertake the leisure pursuit of miniature golf or 'crazy golf'. Often popular at seaside resorts.
Site used for the maintenance of aircraft.
A building, usually housing electrical or electronic equipment, used for gathering and disseminating information. Use specific type where known.
Partly subterranean operations rooms for the lighting arrays of the various types of bombing decoys in use during the Second World War.

A building, often with underground rooms, used to receive all reports of aircraft locations, to assimilate and assess this information in order to provide the most accurate possible picture to the Operations Room of a fighter or bomber Group.
An observation tower is a structure used to provide panoramic views of the surrounding area. They are often used as attractions at seaside resorts e.g. Blackpool Tower.
A site equipped for passive or active defence against an airborne enemy assault.
A site equipped for active defensive action against an airborne enemy assault.
Sites, buildings or structures involved in passive air defence, usually by forcing hostile aircraft to fly high or drop their bombs on the wrong targets. Use more specific term.
A site comprising a system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft. Use more specific type where known.

Sites used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for sites associated with military installations. For non-military sites use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
A building or room where nets are made
Construction works for the production of rigid or dirigible airships.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
Accommodation and facilities for aircrew away from the main RAF airfield.
A room used for the ritual cleaning of the body prior to burial
A large tract of land covered with trees and interspersed with open areas of land. Traditionally forests were owned by the monarchy and had their own laws.
An arrangement of railway tracks, stations and other buildings that together form a railway transport system.
A well with a superstructure, either partially or wholly enclosed with an access door, designed to protect the water source.
An open area of prepared ground used for practising putting with golf clubs.
A low lying area of land that is usually waterlogged at all times and is flooded in wet weather.
A field covered with herbage for the grazing of livestock.
A site used for the manufacturing of steel. Use more specific type where known.
A tall, hollow pipe, usually cast-iron, resembling a lamp-post. Used to ventilate sewer systems.
An archaeological unit of soil in a horizontal plane which may seal features or be cut through by other features.

Type of furnace used in the glass industry to pre-heat glass in crucibles, prior to the main melt. This may have been a separtate structure, or may have been part of the main furnace. All periods from the Roman onwards.
The position of a fire in a wood-fuelled furnace. All periods from the Iron Age  to the 17th century.

In the glass industry, a furnace of Lorraine Type, comprising a central rectangular melting furnace with ancillary structures at each corner, adjacent to the fires. Post-Mediaeval until superceded by coal-fired furnaces.
In the glass industry this is bench-like structure within the melting-furnace on which crucibles are placed.

This is a pit used in the glass industry for the production of cylinder glass. The only surviving examle in England is at the Hartley Wood Glasworks, Sunderland. It is a feature of 19th century and later glassworks
A building or site used to assess the mechanical state of a vehicle.
An area of a site or building providing a stable base for the firing of artillery pieces.
A vehicle or aircraft placed at the entrance to a site as a symbolic guardian.
A venue, with a boxing ring and associated facilities, which is used to train for and undertake amateur or professional boxing.
A small transportable hangar built by the Teesdie Bridge and Engineering Company. Mainly used on RNAS airfields for folding wing aircraft.
Similar in design to the FROMSON HANGAR but designed to drawing number 3752/43 and used for storing aircraft with small wingspans.
A plastic covered tunnel designed to protect vulnerable plants from the weather and allow vegetables to be grown out of season
Similar in design to the Callender Hangar but with a reduced height of 17ft. Built to Air Ministry drawing number 17346/40.
A two-storey watch office similar in design to drawing number 1959/34 but constructed completely from concrete. A large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
A clock with special mechanisms and dials to display astonomical information.
20th century plant for separating minerals using variations in water-repellent properties under controlled chemical conditions. Survives as ruins of buildings or tanks.
18th-19th century stone-lined pit which held the balance bob for a pump-rod or flat-rod system. It includes examples where the surviving feature is a pillar for the bearing, rather than the pit.
Residues from ore-processing operations; intact tips and deposits may preserve considerable evidence on the processes used. A high rpoportion have been destroyed by reprocessing.
A linear open working along a lode vein, worked directly from the surface. Survives as a gully or ravine, normally with closed ends.
Factory producing asbestos sheeting and or asbestos fibre.
A building housing a fan used for the ventilation of mines
A building housing a double inlet fan that was used for the ventillation of mine shafts
Buildings associated with the extaction of uranium from its pitchblende or copper ores.
Plant for the processing of uranium ores, such as pitchblende. Uranium is the principal extract, but radium may also be recovered as a by-product
Mine for the extraction of bismuth, which usually occurs in small quantities in the ores of other metal ores, particularly lead, and some copper ores.
Any building, group of buildings, or site at which tungsten ores have been converted to sodium tungstate by means of the Oxland Process. This was first used at Drakewalls Mine, Cornwall, in 1850.
Any building, group of buildings, or site in which antimony was smelted. Mainly 18th century.
A building housing an electric powered ventilation fan for use in deep mine shafts
An mill in which manganese was ground to a powder between two horizontal millstones.
An ore works at which gold was separated from the ore by the addition of mercury.
A long building with a louvred roof in which silver is refined using the Pattinson Process, which had been developed in the 1830s.

Any building or site in which silver was refined and/or extracted by smelting, cupellation, liquation or by the Parkes Process. IA-C20. Don't use for lead or copper smelters at which silver has been extracted unless silver-related features survive.
Works for the extrusion of aluminium and for creating aluminium products.
A building housing a steam driven ventilation fan used in mines
A zinc smelting furnace patented by William Champion of Bristol in 1738 for the reduction of zinc from zinc oxide by means of condensing.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
A site, building or factory where geologically-derived brine is used for the production of salt.
A coastal site producing salt by boiling of unconcentrated seawater in a PANHOUSE, normally using coal fuel.  Foreshore BRINE TANKS may also be present
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, followed by boiling of the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
A coastal site producing salt by scraping up salt-impregnated sand and silt, leeching out the salt to produce a concentrated brine, then boiling in 'saltcotes' (small huts containing lead pans)
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, without any boiling stage
A shallow pond containing salt water and used for the manufacture of salt through the evaporation process. For metal vessels associated with the DIRECT BOILING and SLEECHING SALT WORKS use SALT PAN.
A coastal site producing salt by dissolving rocksalt or other impure salt in seawater, then boiling the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
A building containing pans in which salt water or brine was boiled to produce salt.

TERM: Royal Flying Corps Side Opening Aircraft Hangar

SCOPE_NOTE: A ventilating fan house with an expanding chimney.
An electric fan used for the ventilation of mines.
A building housing an electric powered mine ventilation fan.
A channel carrying overflow water past a dam. Early 19th century onwards.
A bridge used for carrying liquids, usually water, although sometimes oil, in a pipeline over a river. Mid 19th century onwards.
A pond used for dissipating heat by evaporation from steam engine condensate. Mid 19th century to mid 20th century.
A site, building or factory where seawater is used in the production of salt.
A multi-level structure designed to simulate tall buildings to allow firefighters to practice firefighting and rescue techniques
An impulse water turbine comprising a wheel with hemispherical cups arranged around the circumference using high water pressure to revolve the wheel.
A pit used to bury a large number of people who have died, or been killed, either as a result of warfare, epidemics or natural disasters.
An inclined ramp of earth, stone or brick used to deliver fuel to the firing hole of a kiln. Mediaeval and later.
Series of machines for mechanically slaking lime. 20th century.
A quarry for the extraction of Soapstone (also known as steatite or soaprock), a metamorphic rock largely composed of the mineral talc and rich in magnesium.
A quarry for the extraction of Serpentine, a major metamorphic mineral which is easily polished and easily carved. A major variety, lizardite, is found in Cornwall.
A complex of buildings where barytes is processed for industrial use.
A mechanically operated display board used in greyhound racing, which showed the state of the Tote, or cumulative betting on individual greyhounds.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of rugby.
A building or room used for the repair and maintenance of machinery in a large complex, such as a hospital, school or factory.
A building or group of buildings used for the raising of mink, a semi-aquatic mammal which is farmed for its fur.
A place of worship for the followers of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints
A building housing one end of an underwater telegraph cable.
A 19th century ore processing works which processed the waste material from a mine.
Mediaeval-17th century mining method which involved exploiting an exposed surface vein. Rarely associated with waste.
