A site where chalk is extracted from the ground.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.

A gate, made of wood, used as a livestock barrier by continuing a fence line across a river or stream. The gate usually consists of a series of  droppers, that can float up and down depending on water levels, attached to a length of cable or wooden pole.
A marker stone used to demarcate the boundaries of peat cutting grounds and indicate who held the rights for each particular parcel of land.

A light timber framed building usually with brick panels which rests on a timber frame with jacking points; should ground subsidence occur the structure could be jacked to a level position. Usually found in the Cheshire Salt Field.
An area of land used for producing renewable energy, which can comprise a solar farm, wind turbines or biomass facility
A graduated post or pole adjacent to an area at risk of flooding to indicate the depth of water during a flood.
A plaque attached onto, or a line incised into, a wall face or other surface to indicate the height of flood water inundation.
A site where aircraft are stored, dismantled and processed for the recovery of serviceable parts.

A trench dug through topsoil in an arable field in order to extract underlying clay which was then spread on the field and ploughed in to improve soil fertility. Usually found in peaty soil areas such as the Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire fenlands.
A kiln in the form of a pit dug into the earth which was used for the the production of white coal prior to the Industrial Revolution.
A place where silicate rock was extracted to be shaped for use as whetstones. Examples can be found in Derbyshire and the Blackdown Hills in Devon.
A type of kiln, usually built into banking, with a stone lining that was used to produce white coal which was used as fuel in the lead smelting process.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A shallow outdoor pool, usually rectangular in shape filled with water which when frozen was used for the sport of Curling.

A pit dug to extract Sarsen stones from the superficial geology in which they occur. They range in size from one dug for the extraction of a single boulder to pits from which multiple boulders are extracted & date from the Neolitic to the mid 20th century
An unroofed structure, found on military airfields, protected by brick walls and earth banks for shelter during air raids.
A standard latine block on RAF airfields.
A very long trough laid between the rails of a railway track to allow a suitably equiped steam engine to scoop up water whilst in motion.
A structure for fuelling railway steam locomotives with coal, usually by dropping coal under gravity from an adjacent raised platform.
An 18th Century term for an inn, tavern or coffeehouse where men could meet in secret to socialize and have sex.
A channel in the intertidal zone cleared of large stones and boulders used for the launching and landing of small boats.
The second school in the three tier system of education teaching children from the ages of nine to twelve.
The first school in the three tier system of education teaching children up to the age of nine.
The third school in the three tier system of education teaching children from the age of thirteen until the end of GCSEs or sixth form.
A trench dug into the ground for the purpose of growing plants.  Bedding trenches are often, but not exclusively, associated with vineyards.

Antiquity stars were used on training ranges to indicate areas off limits to troops. They marked the locations of scheduled archaeological features such as barrows, promontory forts and Iron Age forts.

Catchwork or catch-meadow systems diverted water along a series or channels or gutters, often arranged in parallel. They were caused to overflow or included openings to spread water downslope, to irrigate combe sides and encourage growth.
Individual tree, of note for its historical or landscape associations. For named trees, use NAMED TREE
A sloping surface used for people to ski down, either on a snow-covered mountain or on a specially made surface or structure.
Housing for social tenants, provided by a local authority or a housing association (a not-for-profit organisation that owns, lets and manages rented housing).
A structure built to trap or kill otters.

An informal garden area belonging to a vicarage.
A site where raw sugar cane is processed into refined sugar.

A workshop used by a millwright.
A place where chronometers are manufactured.
A post set up alongside a railway to mark the miles to and from a place.
An artificial trough or valley through a hill, carrying at its base a tramway.
A building associated with a Sufi order.
A congregation hall for Muslim commemoration of Muharram.

A structure for fuelling railway steam locomotives with coal. A more advanced type of Coaling Stage where coal wagons are lifted up and physically turned upside down to empty their contents into a raised bunker above the tracks.
A private level crossing which provides access between land and a public highway or between land that is under common occupation but divided by the railway line.
A quarry for the extraction of ganister, a hard fine-grained quartz-arenite (sandstone) cemented with silica, used in the manufacture of silica bricks commonly used to line furnaces.
Structure at an iron works where sintered iron ore, coke and other ingredients are prepared for delivery to the blast furnace.
A tall stone or brick building or iron structure used to lift iron ore and coke to the top of iron works blast furnace, which are loaded from the top.
Debris from salvaging activities on wreck sites.
A site, often just an area of the shore, used for the dismantling of redundant or irreparable vessels.

A plant where iron ore is prepared prior to its use in a blast furnace. Ground iron ores are blended with coke dust, fluxes and furnace dust and heated at over 1,000 degrees Celsius to form a clinker-type material which is charged into the furnace with coke and limestones to reduce the quantity of coke needed and to utilise waste materials.

A Cowper Stove consists of vertical tanks, heated by gas burners, which utilises gas obtained from the exhaust of a blast furnace. A widely-used system for generating hot blast which was patented by Edward Cowper in 1857.
A site where iron is further processed, with other ingredients to produce different specifications of steel before being cast in preparation for shaping.
Site where micaceous haematite was mined for use in rust-resistant paint. Particular to the Hennock-Lustleigh area of Devon where it was known as 'Shiny Ore'.
A trackway through blanket bog constructed to create a dry route. Formed by removing peat to link  	areas already eroded to the granite bedrock.
A flat slab of granite with a central hole, which is set into the main wall of a leat. It acts as a sluice, to  	maintain an optimum supply of water to a subsidiary leat.
A bridge over or under a Railway, allowing access between two parcels of land.
An anti tank obstacle in the form of a post, often of concrete or steel, inserted upright into the ground.
A site where briquets are manufactured
A structure or building, decorated or modified to disguise its true function or conceal its placement.
A building where horses and carriages were exhibited for sale.
A house associated with a complex in which the master of an establishment, such as a workhouse, is accommodated.
A site showing evidence, including floral and faunal remains, of ancient environments.
An opening in a wall at ground level with a lintel across the top allowing sheep to pass through put preventing the movement of larger animals like horses and cattle.
A slope on a tramway system, usually with rails, along which wagons and/or materials can be moved between two relatively flat stretches of tramway.
A pole used to support the overhead electric cable on a tramway
A marker placed above a buried underground telegraph cable.
A factory with specialized machinery for the manufacturing of paper bags.
A mine used for the extraction of limestone.

Woodland believed to have existed since at least 1600 in England and in England defined as such by Natural England. Usually managed for timber, coppice etc and often contains dividing banks, trackways, charcoal burning platforms etc.
A school, usually catering to children of primary school age (4-11) situated in a village setting.
A brick or concrete structure built to the design of Air Ministry drawing number 13241/41,  housing a transformer on a military airfield.
An access cover for a drain allowing water to flow through it but providing a strong enough surface for pedestrians and vehicles to pass over without falling into the drain.
A well providing water rich in minerals
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem, commonly known as the Knights Hospitaller.
A farm established and/or run by a charity, often endowed by a bequest from an individual benefactor for this use.

Fen cottages are small, 1.5 storey, low-status vernacular dwellings constructed of local materials, usually timber-framed with infills of brick, clay lump or wattle and daub panels. Fen cottages are specifically associated with waterborne or water-adjacent smallholder activity that proliferated in the newly-drained fen landscape in the 18th and 19th centuries, intrinsic to the landscape character of the Fens.
A settlement located on or near a river or within marshy landscapes. This type of settlement are raised on piles to prevent flooding.
A large, underground or surface-level excavation from which a tunnel boring machine can begin its journey.
A pit used for the manufacture of charcoal.

Small square or rectangular building, platform or roofed structure, sited at or near the winning post of a horse racing course and designed to provide the race judge with a clear view of the finish line.
A factory used for the manufacture of boxes.
A remnant of an archaeological intervention that still remains visible in the landscape.
A workshop for the small-scale production of saddles.
An establishment where clothes and other textiles can be taken to be cleaned by processes that use a solvent other than water.
A gun, usually fired remotely by means of an electric current, formerly used to signal a specific time of day to inform the local inhabitants or workers in an area.
A dock used for landing fish from a fishing fleet. Usually associated with buildings for processing the fish, ice warehouses and a market.
An institution designed to house 'fallen women' and to restore them to society through religious instruction and moral education.
A building used for the temporary accommodation of vulnerable women particularly those escaping domestic violence.
An area of a park or garden, often in the form of a green or platform, where dancing can take place.
A building used to house tools.
A runway with fencing or barriers down either side used to safely move livestock from one area of a site to another.

A type of Roman temple, usually found in the north-western provinces of the Roman Empire. Romano Celtic temples differ in form from rectangular Classical temples but being either square or octagonal with a central cella rising above a surrounding ambulatory.
